name: Zip Zap Zop
description: Classic circle energy-passing warmup that trains focus, eye contact, and instant response under a simple rule set.
instructions: Stand in a circle. Player 1 claps/points at someone and says 'Zip'. That person immediately points at someone else saying 'Zap', the next says 'Zop', then back to 'Zip', continuing the cycle. Keep the rhythm fast; make clear eye contact before passing. If someone hesitates, says the wrong word, or breaks rhythm, restart (or they do a fun 'shame walk' around the circle and rejoin). Push tempo up as the group warms up.
origin: Theatre warmup tradition; ubiquitous in improv and drama classes
variations: Add 'Boing' to bounce a pass back; add extra sound words traveling the circle simultaneously; eliminate players to a final duel.

name: Pass the Clap
description: Circle warmup where two players clap in perfect unison, passing the clap around the circle; trains shared timing, presence, and giving/receiving attention.
instructions: Stand in a circle. Turn to your neighbor, make eye contact, and try to clap at exactly the same moment they do. The neighbor then turns to the next person and repeats, sending the clap around the circle. Aim for perfect unison rather than speed at first, then accelerate. Add rules: a double clap reverses direction; you can clap across the circle to anyone you make eye contact with.
origin: Standard improv/theatre warmup; taught at Hoopla and most schools
variations: Send two claps in opposite directions and watch the collision; 'whoosh/whoa/zap' variants layer in more signals.

name: Big Booty
description: Rhythmic chanting name/number game; trains keeping rhythm under pressure and graceful public failure.
instructions: Stand in a circle. One player is 'Big Booty'; everyone else numbers off (Number 1, Number 2, etc.). Establish a group rhythm (clap-stomp or sway) and chant the intro ('Big Booty, Big Booty, Big Booty — aww yeah'). Big Booty starts: 'Big Booty, Number 3', then Number 3 must immediately call their own number then someone else's ('Number 3, Number 7') without breaking rhythm. Anyone who flubs moves to the last seat and everyone re-numbers; the goal is to dethrone Big Booty. Celebrate mistakes loudly.
origin: American improv warmup tradition (widely used at UCB and colleges)
variations: Speed rounds; gibberish numbers; double-time rhythm.

name: Bunny Bunny
description: High-energy nonsense chant warmup that pushes players past self-consciousness through committed silliness.
instructions: Circle up. One player starts pulsing their hands by their face chanting 'bunny bunny bunny bunny', then throws 'BUNNY!' across the circle with a big gesture to another player. That player becomes the bunny and chants while their two neighbors become 'wings', flapping toward them chanting too. The receiver then passes the bunny on. Full vocal and physical commitment is the only rule; play until the group is loud and loose.
origin: Improv warmup tradition; popularized in US theaters (title of Gilda Radner biography play)
variations: Change the chanted word; add competing animals traveling the circle.

name: Whoosh
description: Imaginary ball of energy passed around the circle with sounds and gestures; trains offers, acceptance, and physical commitment.
instructions: Circle up. Pass a 'whoosh' (sweeping both hands toward your neighbor with the sound 'whoosh'). Add rules one at a time: 'Whoa' (hands up) bounces it back the other way; 'Zap' sends it across the circle; 'Groovalicious' makes everyone dance in place; 'Freak out' makes everyone run to new spots in the circle. Keep energy high; mistakes are celebrated with a group 'ahhh' and play continues.
variations: Let the group invent new calls; play silent with gestures only.

name: Mind Meld
description: Two players count '3-2-1' and simultaneously say a word, then repeat trying to converge on the same word; the canonical group-mind exercise.
instructions: Two players face each other. Count '3, 2, 1' together and each says any word. Then, thinking of a word 'between' the two words just said, count down again and say new words simultaneously. Repeat until both say the same word at the same moment — the group celebrates ('Mind meld!'). Rules: no repeating already-said words, no pre-negotiating. Play as a whole group in a circle with rotating pairs.
origin: Improv warmup tradition; staple at UCB/iO
variations: Whole-group version: anyone steps forward to pair; 'Hive Mind' where entire group counts down together until everyone converges.

name: Count to 21
description: The group tries to count to 21 with one voice at a time and no order; trains shared focus, patience, and reading the room.
instructions: Group stands in a circle, often with eyes closed or gazes lowered. Anyone may say the next number, but if two people speak at once, the count restarts at 1. No system or order is allowed — players must sense when to speak. Continue until the group reaches 21. Debrief: what did it feel like when the group rushed vs. settled?
variations: Count higher; recite the alphabet; do it walking around the room.

name: Hot Spot
description: One player sings in the center until a teammate tags them out with a new song; trains support, association, and bold commitment.
instructions: Group forms a tight circle. One player jumps to the center and starts singing any song loudly. As soon as the song reminds anyone of another song, they tag the center player out and start singing theirs. Never leave someone stranded too long — the group's job is rescue. Commit fully even if you don't know the words or can't sing. Continue 5-10 minutes at high pace.
origin: iO/UCB warmup tradition; standard Harold-team warmup
variations: Monologue Hot Spot (rants instead of songs); themed rounds (one-genre songs).

name: Bippity Bippity Bop
description: Center player tries to catch circle players off-guard with commands requiring instant 3-person poses; trains reaction speed and teamwork.
instructions: One player stands in the center of the circle. They approach anyone and say 'bippity bippity bop' — the target must say 'bop' before the phrase ends or they replace the center. If the center just says 'bop', the target must stay silent. Add poses: center calls 'Elephant!' (target makes a trunk, neighbors make ears) or 'Palm tree', 'Toaster', 'James Bond' — the three players must form the pose before a count of five. Whoever fails becomes the center.
origin: Theatre/camp game tradition adopted by improv
variations: Invent new three-person poses with the group; eliminate to a final three.

name: Samurai
description: Stylized sword-strike circle game with loud 'HA!' shouts; builds energy, eye contact, and full-body vocal commitment.
instructions: Circle up. One player raises an imaginary sword overhead shouting 'HA!', then slashes it down pointing at another player ('HA!'). The two neighbors of the target simultaneously slash sideways toward the target's belly ('HA!') while the target raises the sword overhead, then the target sends it onward. Keep shouts loud and movements crisp. Players who hesitate or mis-fire are eliminated or simply restart.
variations: Slow-motion samurai; whisper samurai; elimination rounds.

name: Eight Things
description: Players rapid-fire list eight items in a category chosen by the group; trains fast, judgment-free idea generation.
instructions: Circle up. The group points at one player and assigns a category ('8 brands of cereal!', '8 things you'd say to a dragon!'). The player lists eight things as fast as possible — quality irrelevant, momentum everything — while the group counts each answer and then cheers ('8 things!'). That player then assigns a new category to someone else. Coach players to say the first thing in their head; wrong or absurd answers are wins.
origin: Improv warmup tradition; common at UCB
variations: Solo version: set a timer and list 8 things in self-chosen categories aloud; '5 Things' with elaborate descriptions of each item.

name: Crazy Eights Shakeout
description: Physical shakeout counting down from 8 on each limb; raises energy and drops physical tension before scene work.
instructions: Standing, shake your right hand 8 times counting aloud '1-2-3-4-5-6-7-8!', then left hand 8, right foot 8, left foot 8. Repeat the cycle with counts of 4, then 2, then 1, getting faster and louder, ending with a big group cheer or jump. Encourage full volume — the point is shared abandon.
variations: Count in gibberish or in character voices.

name: Word Association Circle
description: Players pass single-word associations around a circle as fast as possible; the foundational free-association drill.
instructions: Circle up. Player 1 says any word to their neighbor ('ocean'); the neighbor instantly says the first word it triggers ('wave') to the next person, and so on around the circle. Coach: no pausing to be clever, no censoring, no pre-planning while waiting. If the pace drags, restart with a new word. Variation 'Word Ball': throw an imaginary ball across the circle with each association so order is unpredictable.
origin: Classic psychology/improv crossover; in every improv curriculum
variations: Solo version aloud while walking; 'association chain' where you must explain the link; opposites-only round.

name: Name Six
description: A player must name six items in a category before an object passes around the circle back to them; trains listing under time pressure.
instructions: Sit or stand in a circle with a ball or shoe. One player in the center closes their eyes while the object passes; when they say 'stop', whoever holds it gets a category from the center player ('six pizza toppings'). The object immediately continues around the circle and the holder must name six items before it returns to them. Fail and you swap into the center. Keep categories everyday and play fast.
origin: Party/camp game adopted as improv warmup
variations: Name 3 for kids; harder abstract categories for advanced groups.

name: Look Up, Look Down
description: Eye-contact elimination game; desensitizes players to direct eye contact and builds ensemble connection.
instructions: Circle up, everyone looking at the floor. Leader calls 'Look up!' and everyone immediately looks at one specific person's face. If that person is looking back at you, you both shout ('Dude!' or scream dramatically) and step out (or swap places). Leader calls 'Look down', then repeats. Play until two remain, or play no-elimination where caught pairs simply swap spots.
variations: Caught pairs perform a 30-second two-line scene before rejoining.

name: The Shakes
description: Players develop rhythmic tremors in a body part and 'throw' them across the circle; trains physical commitment and giving/receiving offers.
instructions: Circle up. One player starts a rhythmic shake in one body part (a hand, a knee, the head), letting it grow. Making eye contact, they 'throw' the shakes to someone across the circle, who 'catches' it in the same body part, lets it migrate somewhere new, then throws it on. Coach full commitment — the shake should look involuntary and be fun to watch.
variations: Add sound to each shake; shakes intensify each pass until full-body.

name: Danish Clapping
description: Partner clapping-and-gesture mirror game; trains rhythm, peripheral awareness, and celebrating mistakes.
instructions: Face a partner. On a shared rhythm: (1) both slap thighs, (2) each throws both arms up, left, or right, (3) clap. If your arm gestures happen to match, give a high ten and shout 'Hey!' then find a new partner (or keep score). Keep the three-beat rhythm steady; matches are luck, so the game teaches you to enjoy outcomes you don't control.
origin: Scandinavian children's game adopted by improv (taught at Hoopla)
variations: Speed up each round; tournament style with cheering crowds.

name: Creatures of the Deep
description: A physical 'telephone' game where an impression of a sea creature mutates as it passes around the circle; trains copying, exaggeration, and acceptance.
instructions: Circle up. The leader turns to their neighbor and performs a brief full-body sea creature impression with sound. The neighbor copies it as exactly as they can to the next person, and so on around the circle, letting the impression naturally drift and mutate. Start several creatures going at once for chaos. Debrief: copying IS creating — drift happens by itself.
variations: Any animal category; emotions instead of creatures.

name: Volcano
description: On a called word, the whole group has five seconds to physically build that object together; trains instant wordless collaboration.
instructions: Players mill around the room. The leader calls an object ('Volcano!', 'Microwave!', 'Eiffel Tower!') and counts down from five. Before zero, the entire group must arrange their bodies into one collective version of the object — no talking or negotiating allowed. Hold it, appreciate it, then resume walking. Repeat with escalating absurdity.
variations: Small teams compete to form the object; add sound effects.

name: Meet and Greet Walkabout
description: Players walk the room greeting each other under changing relational frames (best friends, rivals, exes); trains instant relationship endowment.
instructions: Everyone walks the room. The leader calls a frame: 'Greet each other as long-lost best friends!' Players greet whoever they meet in that frame for ~30 seconds. New frames: suspicious neighbors, superheroes meeting fans, ex-partners, proud parents, spies exchanging codes. Coach players to notice how body, voice, and eye contact change with each relationship.
origin: Hoopla Impro beginners curriculum; common drama warmup
variations: Greet in gibberish; greet at status 1-10.

name: Yipee
description: Players run around jumping and shouting 'YIPEE!' together; a pure joy-and-silliness icebreaker that lowers stakes for everything after.
instructions: Everyone moves around the room. When you approach another player, make eye contact, and jump in the air together shouting 'YIPEE!'. Advanced rule: both players must either jump or stay grounded together — sense it, don't signal it. Final stage: the whole group converges into one synchronized jumping mass.
variations: Replace YIPEE with character catchphrases.

name: Wild West
description: Circle game passing 'YE-HAH!' with cowboy gestures plus call-outs that change the pattern; trains energy, listening, and rule agility.
instructions: Circle up. Pass 'YE-HAH!' around the circle with a big arm-swing in your best western accent. Add calls anyone can use: 'HIGH-BARN!' reverses direction; 'BANDITS!' means everyone runs to a new spot in the circle. Invent more calls with the group as you go ('SALOON!' everyone mimes drinking). Keep volume and commitment maximal.
variations: Re-theme to any genre (pirates, soap opera, sci-fi).

name: Anyone Who
description: Circle chair-swap game driven by self-disclosure prompts; doubles as icebreaker and vulnerability practice.
instructions: Sit in a circle of chairs with one fewer chair than players; one player stands in the middle and says 'Anyone who...' plus something true about themselves ('...has a brother', '...has cried at an ad'). Everyone for whom it's true must dash to a new chair (not adjacent); the middle player grabs a seat, leaving a new caller. Encourage prompts that escalate from trivial to genuinely revealing.
origin: Camp/teambuilding game used across improv classes
variations: 'Big Wind Blows' phrasing; truths must be things you've never told the group.

name: Mr. Hit
description: A slow 'zombie' stalks players who must save themselves by calling another player's name; trains name recall and calm under approach.
instructions: Circle up; learn everyone's names first. One player walks zombie-like toward any other player. The target must call out another player's name before being touched — the named player becomes the zombie's new target's savior chain continues. If touched before naming someone, you become the zombie. Speed and panic increase as the game continues.
variations: Two zombies at once; zombie moves at normal speed for advanced groups.

name: Yes, And
description: The foundational agreement drill: partners build an idea by accepting each statement and adding new information.
instructions: Pairs. Player A makes a simple statement ('We're painting the fence today'). Player B responds starting literally with 'Yes, and...' — accepting A's reality and adding one new piece of information. Continue alternating, every line starting 'Yes, and', until the idea reaches a natural peak (plan a holiday, design a restaurant, plot a heist). Debrief on the moments someone secretly said no (blocking) or added nothing (hedging). Then replay the same conversation with 'Yes, but' and 'No' rounds to feel the difference.
origin: Core improv principle; codified by Spolin/Johnstone lineages, taught everywhere
variations: 'Yes, because' for justification practice; group planning version ('Let's throw a party!'); physical yes-and where offers are mimed not spoken.

name: Yes, Let's!
description: Group acceptance game: any player proposes an activity and the whole group enthusiastically does it; trains embodied agreement.
instructions: Group mills about. Any player calls out 'Let's all... [ride horses / be librarians shushing / swim through jello]!' Everyone responds 'YES, LET'S!' and commits fully to the activity until someone calls a new one. No vetoes, no half-hearted miming. Coach the group to notice how fast enthusiasm makes even weak ideas fun. Variation 'or Rather Not': players may decline with 'No, let's not' to practice graceful rejection — then return to pure yes.
variations: Themed rounds (all activities at the beach); silent version with gesture invitations.

name: Word at a Time Story
description: Players tell a single story contributing exactly one word each in turn; the purest drill for moment-to-moment listening and surrendering control.
instructions: Two players (or a circle) tell a story one word per person: 'Once' / 'upon' / 'a' / 'time' / 'there'... Keep grammar intact and the pace conversational. Coach: don't plan your next word; serve the sentence, not your idea. End sentences confidently rather than spiraling. Circle version: go around 10+ players. Pair version: aim for a complete tiny story with a beginning, middle, and end. If stuck, shout 'Again!' and restart with momentum.
origin: Keith Johnstone tradition (Impro for Storytellers); universal curriculum item
variations: Word-at-a-time letter ('Dear Sir...'); word-at-a-time proverb (Wise Wise Wise); two-headed expert answering interview questions one word each.

name: Story Swap
description: One player tells a story until a signal, then the partner continues from the exact word; trains deep listening and seamless co-creation.
instructions: Pairs, plus a director (or timer). Player A starts telling an improvised story. When the director claps and calls 'Swap!', Player B continues instantly from the precise point — mid-sentence, mid-word — matching tone and content. Swap every 10-30 seconds. The story should sound like one teller. Coach against planning ahead and against resetting the story at each swap.
variations: Solo practice: swap between two character narrator voices yourself on a timer.

name: Conducted Story
description: A conductor points among a line of storytellers who must continue one seamless story; trains attention, instant pickup, and group narrative.
instructions: 4-6 players stand in a line; a conductor faces them. Get a story title from the group. The conductor points at any player, who narrates the story until the conductor switches to someone else — mid-sentence switches are the point. The story must flow as if told by one voice. Performance variation 'Story Story Die': players who stumble, repeat, or break grammar are eliminated with a dramatic death scene voted by the audience.
variations: Genre switches called mid-story; sung version ('Greatest Hits').

name: Yeah Yeah Yeah
description: Partners co-tell a shared 'memory', enthusiastically taking the story from each other with 'Yeah yeah yeah!'; trains enthusiastic agreement and shared ownership of ideas.
instructions: Pairs. Player A starts 'Do you remember that time we...' and begins a fictional shared memory. Player B interrupts with an enthusiastic 'Yeah yeah yeah!' (big body language) and continues the memory as their own, adding detail. Keep stealing the story back and forth every few sentences with full enthusiasm. The story belongs to both of you; treat every addition as exactly what happened.
variations: Do it as exaggerating fishermen; as a couple telling their 'how we met' story.

name: Three Sentence Story
description: Players tell a complete story — beginning, middle, end — in exactly three sentences; trains economy and narrative shape.
instructions: In a circle, give each player a title ('The Jealous Lighthouse Keeper'). They must tell a complete story in exactly three sentences: sentence 1 establishes a character and routine, sentence 2 breaks the routine, sentence 3 resolves it. No run-on cheating. Go around several times, increasing speed. Debrief on what makes a story feel complete with so little.
variations: One-sentence stories; six-episode version expanding each sentence into a scene.

name: Story Spine
description: Fill-in-the-blank story skeleton ('Once upon a time... Every day... But one day... Because of that... Until finally...') used as a drill for instant well-structured stories.
instructions: Alone or around a circle, tell a story using the fixed spine, one clause per turn: 'Once upon a time ___. Every day ___. But one day ___. Because of that ___. Because of that ___. Because of that ___. Until finally ___. And ever since then ___.' Take any suggestion as the topic. Coach: 'because of that' must be a true consequence, not a new event. Repeat daily solo with random nouns as prompts for fluency.
origin: Kenn Adams (Adventure Theater), popularized via Pixar
variations: Spine in a genre; spine about your own day (true story version); group one-clause-each.

name: One Minute Life Story
description: Partners tell their real life story in 60 seconds while the other practices pure listening, then recalls it back.
instructions: Pairs. Player A tells their actual life story in one minute; B listens with full attention — no interrupting, minimal nodding, no rehearsing a response. B then repeats back as much as they can ('You were born in..., then...'). Swap. Debrief: what did being truly heard feel like? What did you miss while 'listening'? Used to open courses because it builds trust fast.
origin: Hoopla Impro beginners curriculum; counseling-skills crossover
variations: Story of your name; story of one scar; 30-second re-tell where B tells A's story in first person.

name: Wise Wise Wise
description: The circle invents 'ancient proverbs' one word at a time, sealing each with a group bow; trains collective sentence-building and confident nonsense.
instructions: Circle up. Build a proverb one word per player: 'A' / 'wet' / 'dog' / 'never' / 'doubts' / 'the' / 'moon'. When a sentence lands with proverb-like finality, the whole group intones 'Wise, wise, wise...' and bows. Coach: short words keep it alive; aim for the sentence to END (players love extending forever). Nonsense delivered with gravity is the comedy engine.
variations: Fortune cookie fortunes; horoscopes; advice column answers.

name: I Am a Tree
description: One player strikes a pose declaring what they are; others join the picture one at a time with complementary offers; trains supporting ideas over inventing new ones.
instructions: Circle around an open space. Player 1 steps in, poses, and declares 'I am a tree.' Player 2 joins with something that complements ('I am an apple hanging from the tree'), then Player 3 ('I am the worm in the apple'). Classic version: the starter chooses one element to stay ('The worm stays'), others clear, and the worm restarts a new picture. Speed version (Martha Game): build pictures of 5-8 people as fast as possible with zero thinking. Coach: add to THIS picture, don't import your own idea.
origin: Theatre games tradition; in nearly every curriculum
variations: Add a line of dialogue from each element; pictures must be locations and two players start a scene in them.

name: Machine
description: Players build a machine one body-part-and-sound at a time; the classic physical 'yes and' and group-mind builder.
instructions: One player starts a repeating mechanical motion with a sound. One at a time, others attach themselves with a complementary repeating motion and sound until the whole group is one machine. Leader can adjust speed ('the machine overheats... slows to a stop'). Themed version: build a 'procrastination machine' or 'love machine' where parts express the theme. Debrief how each person's offer changed the whole.
origin: Viola Spolin (Part of a Whole); Boal's Machine of Rhythms variant
variations: Machine of Rhythms (Boal): build from a rhythm not an object; emotion machines; machine that one player must operate.

name: The Because Game
description: Players extend ideas using 'because', distinguishing offers that deepen a scene (vertical) from ones that merely change topic (horizontal).
instructions: Pairs. A makes a statement ('The bakery is closed today'). B responds 'That's because...' and adds a reason that deepens the situation ('...the baker is testifying in court'). A continues 'And because of that...'. Build a chain of consequence 6-10 links long. Then contrast: replay where each response merely adds an unrelated detail, and feel how the scene goes sideways instead of forward. Use in scenes afterward: every third line must be a 'because' line.
origin: Modern improv pedagogy (Reflex Improv and others)
variations: Solo: respond to podcast/radio lines aloud with 'Yes, and that's because...'.

name: That's Right, Bob
description: Two hosts sell a product, each line beginning 'That's right, Bob!'; trains agreement, enthusiasm, and building on a partner's last idea.
instructions: Pairs play TV shopping hosts selling a suggested product (e.g., a self-stirring mug). Every line must start by enthusiastically validating the partner ('That's right, Bob! And it also...') before adding a new feature, story, or price drop. Keep energy at infomercial pitch. The validation phrase forces genuine listening — you can't 'that's right' something you didn't hear.
variations: Sports commentators; cooking-show hosts; award-show presenters.

name: Presents
description: Johnstone exercise: one player mimes giving an unnamed gift; the receiver defines it with delight; trains making your partner's offers valuable.
instructions: Pairs. A mimes handing B a present (just a shaped box — A does NOT decide what's inside). B opens it and declares what it is with genuine delight ('A ukulele! You remembered!'), then justifies why it's perfect. Swap and repeat rapidly, 10+ gifts. Advanced: receiver lets the size/weight of the mime inform the gift. Coach: the giver gives 'nothing'; the receiver makes it a treasure — this is how offers work in scenes.
variations: Giver names the present and receiver justifies loving it; gifts exchanged in character.

name: It's Tuesday (Overaccepting)
description: One player delivers a mundane line; the partner reacts as if it changes their life; trains treating small offers as important.
instructions: Pairs. A says the most boring line possible ('It's Tuesday', 'The mail came'). B 'overaccepts': reacts with a level-10 emotional response and a monologue justifying why this changes everything ('Tuesday?! Then the inspection is TODAY — I never filed the permits...'). Swap. Coach: the reaction must be specific and justified, not random screaming. Then play scenes where every mundane offer gets treated as significant.
origin: Keith Johnstone (overaccepting); drilled at most schools
variations: Dial reactions 1-10 on command; both players overaccept alternately.

name: The Ad Game
description: A team of ad executives enthusiastically builds a campaign for an absurd product, accepting every idea as genius; trains group yes-and and instant pitching.
instructions: 4-6 players are an ad agency; get a product suggestion (e.g., edible umbrellas). Players pitch ideas rapid-fire — name, slogan, jingle, celebrity endorsement, TV spot — and EVERY idea is met with the whole group shouting 'YES!' and building on it ('And the jingle goes...'). No idea is questioned. End by 'presenting' the full campaign. Coach: speed over quality; agreement creates the comedy.
variations: Campaign for an abstract concept (jealousy); movie-pitch version.

name: New Choice
description: A director bell forces players to instantly replace their last line with a new one, repeatedly; trains infinite optionality and detachment from your first idea.
instructions: Two players scene; a director with a bell (or 'Ding!') can ring after any line. The player must instantly replace that line with a different one ('I brought you flowers' — DING — 'I brought you soup' — DING — 'I sold your car'). The scene continues incorporating whatever survives. Ring 3-5 times in a row sometimes; the third+ choices are where originality lives. Solo version: narrate a story and ding yourself every few sentences.
origin: Theatresports/short-form canon; famous from Whose Line
variations: New emotion ding; new accent ding; physical-action ding.

name: Questions Only
description: Players run a scene speaking only in questions; trains verbal agility and reveals how questions push action.
instructions: Two lines of players; the front pair starts a scene (with a location suggestion) where every line must be a question that advances the scene ('Is this your first time at the embassy?' 'Did the ambassador send for you?'). Statements, hesitations, or non-sequitur questions get you buzzed out; the next player in line jumps in. Keep it flowing, not gotcha — questions should still be offers.
variations: Questions in character; pair version as a rally with scoring like tennis.

name: Last Letter, First Letter
description: Each line of dialogue must begin with the last letter of the partner's previous line; trains listening to the very end of sentences.
instructions: Pairs scene with any suggestion. If A's line ends in '...we should escapE', B's line must start with E ('Every door is locked, though'). Keep scene logic alive — the constraint must not kill the relationship or stakes. Buzz and swap on errors, or just self-correct and continue in practice mode. This forces full listening because you cannot plan your line before their sentence ends.
variations: Alphabet Game (lines start A, B, C... through Z); solo: alternate two characters yourself.

name: Alphabet Scene
description: A 26-line scene where line 1 starts with A, line 2 with B, through Z; trains structure under constraint and graceful handling of hard letters (Q, X).
instructions: Two players, get a letter to start from and a location. Alternate lines, each starting with the next letter of the alphabet, wrapping around to the start letter. Keep the scene emotionally real despite the constraint — relationship first, alphabet second. Q, X, and Z force creativity ('Quite frankly...', 'X-rays don't lie!'). Finish exactly on the 26th line if possible.
variations: 90-second speed alphabet; three-player version; backwards Z-A.

name: World's Worst
description: Players step forward with rapid-fire examples of 'the world's worst [X]'; a punchline-generation drill disguised as a game.
instructions: Players in a back line. Host announces a category: 'World's worst... wedding DJ'. Any player steps forward and performs a 3-10 second snippet of that terrible person ('Up next: the bride's exes — all of them'). Step back; next idea steps out. Keep a popcorn pace; commit physically and vocally, don't just say a joke — be it. No discussion between offers.
variations: Solo with a timer: 10 world's-worsts in 2 minutes aloud; 'World's best' round.

description: Joke-format drill: '185 [suggestion]s walk into a bar...' players improvise puns on the spot; trains joke structure and pun fluency.
instructions: Get a noun suggestion ('185 pencils'). Players step forward one at a time delivering the fixed format: '185 pencils walk into a bar. The bartender says: we don't serve pencils here. The pencils say: [punchline/pun]'. Groans count as wins. Keep volume and confidence even on weak puns — the reps are the point. Run 10-15 jokes per suggestion before switching.
variations: Solo daily reps with random nouns; alternative formats ('Knock knock' chains).

name: Five Things
description: Chant-driven game where a player names five examples of a wild category, elaborating each; trains structured spontaneity with group support.
instructions: Circle chants 'Five things! Five things!' and points at a player, calling a category ('Five ways to annoy a wizard!'). The player gives five rapid answers, the group echoing each with a chant ('That's one!'). Answers should be specific mini-bits, not single words. The player then launches the chant at someone new. Group energy carries weak answers — celebrate everything.
variations: Gibberish round where group 'translates'; themed categories for show prep.

name: Three-Line Scenes
description: Rapid-fire two-person scenes capped at exactly three lines that must establish who, where, and what; the core scene-initiation drill.
instructions: Two lines of players. The front pair plays exactly three lines: A initiates (establishing something concrete), B responds (adding relationship/context), A responds once more (sealing who/where/what). Then 'scene!' and the next pair goes. Coach: name your partner, state the relationship or activity directly, no questions as initiations. Run 20+ scenes so everyone initiates many times. Debrief which initiations gave the most information.
variations: Pair drill back and forth; three-line scenes that must start mid-action; emotion-first initiations.

name: Who What Where
description: Scene drill focused purely on quickly establishing character, relationship, objective, and location in the opening moments.
instructions: Two players, 30-60 seconds: start a scene and establish a clear WHERE and WHO (then in later rounds add WHAT objective) as fast and naturally as possible — through behavior and dialogue, not announcement ('Hand me the wrench' + lying under a car beats 'Here we are in the garage'). Coach ends the scene the moment all elements are clear and asks observers to name them. Rotate quickly through many pairs.
origin: Canadian Improv Games five elements; Spolin Where games
variations: Silent round: establish where/who with zero dialogue; audience guesses.

name: First Line, Last Line
description: A scene must begin with one given line and end with another; trains narrative steering toward a destination without forcing it.
instructions: Collect two unrelated lines of dialogue (from the group or slips of paper). Two players begin a scene with line one and must organically arrive at line two as the final line. Coach: don't rush to the last line — build a real scene whose logic earns it. Debrief: when did the steering show? Run multiple pairs with the same two lines to see different routes.
variations: Audience-written lines drawn blind from a hat (Blind Line Offers) injected mid-scene.

name: Blind Line Offers
description: Players must instantly justify random pre-written lines pulled mid-scene; the classic justification-under-chaos drill.
instructions: Before the scene, collect 10+ lines of dialogue written by the group on slips ('That's not my llama', 'I never learned to read'). Two players scene normally, but at any point the director points at a player, who draws a slip, reads it as their line, and the scene must justify it completely. Coach: react to the line as if your character meant it; the justification is the partner's job too.
origin: Short-form canon (Whose Line 'Scenes from a Hat' family)
variations: Phone-autocorrect version using random book sentences; solo version justifying random lines aloud.

name: Emotional Quadrants
description: The stage is divided into four zones, each assigned an emotion; players' characters snap to the zone's emotion as they move; trains instant emotional shifts with justification.
instructions: Mark four stage quadrants and assign each an emotion (rage, infatuation, terror, joy). Two players scene with any suggestion; whenever a player steps into a quadrant they must play that emotion fully AND justify the shift within the scene's reality. Encourage deliberate crossing to practice shifts. Coach: emotion changes how you feel about the SAME situation — don't change the topic.
setup: floor divided into four zones (tape optional)
variations: Audience assigns emotions; zones change mid-scene; volume quadrants instead of emotions.

name: Emotional Rollercoaster
description: A director calls out emotions during a scene and players must instantly switch while justifying the change; trains emotional flexibility on demand.
instructions: Two players scene from a location suggestion. A side-coach calls emotions every 20-40 seconds ('jealousy!... relief!... disgust!'). Players shift their character's emotional state immediately and justify it inside the scene ('...actually, now that I see the receipt, I'm relieved'). Coach for specificity: resentful not just angry; wistful not just sad. End with a debrief on which emotions felt inaccessible — those are homework.
origin: Improv class canon; Whose Line family
variations: Emotion Replay: play the same 1-minute scene three times in three emotions; sliding-scale rounds (anger level 1 → 10).

name: Boring Line, Emotional Dial
description: Deliver an identical mundane line at many different emotions and intensities; isolates subtext and delivery from content.
instructions: Pick one neutral line ('The bus leaves at noon'). Solo or in pairs, deliver it: loud-angry, quiet-angry (death glare), sobbing, suppressing tears, flirtatious, terrified, triumphant. Then run an intensity ladder on one emotion: level 1 (a flicker) to level 10 (full eruption), finding the distinct levels 3, 5, 7. Partner version: B responds with their own neutral line in a complementary emotion, creating an instant scene. Debrief: meaning lived entirely in delivery.
origin: Acting pedagogy adopted by improv (Theatrefolk and others)
variations: Record yourself solo and review; do it with a single word ('Okay') instead of a sentence.

name: Space Jump
description: Nested scenes: players freeze and new players join, starting fresh scenes from the frozen poses, then unwind back through every scene; trains justification and scene memory.
instructions: Player 1 starts a solo scene. Director calls 'Space jump!'; Player 1 freezes and Player 2 enters, starting a brand-new two-person scene justified by the frozen pose. Continue adding players (3-person, 4-person, 5-person scenes). Then unwind: 'Space jump!' removes the last-added player, and the remaining players must resume the PREVIOUS scene exactly where it left off, until Player 1 finishes their solo scene. Coach: re-enter old scenes with their established reality intact.
variations: Genre per layer; emotion per layer.

name: Freeze Tag
description: Players call 'Freeze!', take over a frozen player's exact body position, and justify it into a completely new scene; the most famous justification drill in improv.
instructions: Two players start a scene with big physicality. Anyone watching may call 'Freeze!', tap one player out, assume their exact pose, and start a totally different scene justified by the two positions. Keep scenes short (30-60s) and physical so poses stay interesting. Coach: the new scene should come FROM the pose, not a pre-planned idea; call freeze on movement, not on punchlines. Blind Freeze variant: callers stand facing away, then turn and must justify whatever they see.
origin: Theatre games tradition; in every improv curriculum
variations: Blind Freeze (no pre-planning possible); Chain Freeze where each new scene must connect thematically.

name: What Are You Doing?
description: A player mimes an action but must answer 'What are you doing?' with something DIFFERENT, which the asker must then perform; trains decoupling words from actions and rapid invention.
instructions: Two players (or a rotating line). A mimes an activity (brushing teeth). B asks 'What are you doing?' A answers with anything EXCEPT the real action ('Wrestling an octopus'). B must immediately mime wrestling an octopus, then A asks B the question. Continue, accelerating. Advanced: answers must start with given initials, or be themed. Eliminate on hesitation, repetition, or describing the actual action.
origin: Drama games tradition; everywhere from camps to ComedySportz
variations: Initials version (answers must use letters from suggestion); themed categories; whole-circle elimination.

name: Party Quirks
description: A host must guess the bizarre secret identities/quirks of arriving party guests; trains character commitment and indirect communication.
instructions: One host leaves the room; three guests each get a secret quirk/identity (a time traveler who's always 10 seconds in the future; a person convinced they're made of glass). Guests arrive one at a time and mingle, playing the quirk fully without stating it. The host plays the party while trying to guess each quirk; correct guesses send that guest home. Coach guests to escalate clues from subtle to broad, and the host to play the scene, not an interrogation.
variations: Job interview version (interviewer guesses applicants' quirks); Press Conference (one player guesses who THEY are from reporters' questions).

name: Press Conference
description: One player holds a press conference without knowing who they are; reporters' questions carry clues until the speaker can guess; trains inference and confident bluffing.
instructions: One player leaves; the group picks who they are and what they've done (e.g., the first squirrel to climb Everest). The player returns and takes questions as that mystery figure. Reporters embed clues in questions ('Was the lack of oxygen harder on your tail?'). The speaker answers in full confident sentences while deducing their identity, ending when they can state who they are. Coach reporters: clue difficulty should ramp down gradually.
variations: Solo practice: answer podcast interview questions as an unknown expert, committing before knowing your angle.

name: Hitchhiker
description: Car passengers progressively adopt each new hitchhiker's character trait; trains observation, imitation, and full-cast character infection.
instructions: Four chairs arranged like a car; three players drive and chat. A hitchhiker with a strong character choice (physical + vocal) is picked up; within a minute, ALL passengers gradually catch the hitchhiker's trait. Once everyone is fully infected, the driver exits, everyone shifts one seat, and a new hitchhiker arrives. Coach: catch the trait organically (justify why you're starting to giggle/whisper/preach), not instantly.
variations: Emotion hitchhikers; status hitchhikers.

name: Sit, Stand, Lie
description: Three players scene while at all times exactly one must sit, one stand, one lie down; trains stage picture awareness and physical give-and-take.
instructions: Three players, any scene suggestion. The rule: at every moment one player sits, one stands, one lies down — when anyone changes position, the others must instantly rebalance, justifying their moves inside the scene. Coach: justify the WHY ('I'll just rest here while you two argue'); keep the scene's story primary. Audience calls out violations in practice.
variations: Levels only (high/medium/low); four players with four postures.

name: Give and Take Focus
description: Spolin focus exercise: players practice deliberately taking and giving stage focus through movement, stillness, and voice.
instructions: Group walks the space neutrally. On 'TAKE', one player (self-selected, only one at a time) does something to seize focus — movement, sound, level change — while everyone else actively gives focus (stillness, orientation toward them). On 'GIVE', the focus-holder passes it deliberately to someone else, who must take it. Then run scenes where the director calls 'give'/'take' to make focus-shifting conscious. Debrief: how do you take focus politely in conversation? How do you give it generously?
origin: Viola Spolin, Improvisation for the Theater
variations: No-caller version where the group self-organizes one-focus-at-a-time.

name: He Said, She Said
description: Players alternate narrating stage directions for their partner who must perform them, then speaking their own lines; trains control-sharing and physical offers.
instructions: Two players. A speaks a line of dialogue, then narrates a stage direction for B ('...she said, slamming the oven door'). B must perform the direction, then speak their own line and narrate a direction for A. Continue. Directions must be performable and in the scene's reality. Coach: give directions that make your partner look interesting; perform received directions fully before speaking.
variations: Directions only round (no dialogue); emotional stage directions.

name: Slide Show
description: A presenter narrates a slideshow whose 'slides' are frozen tableaux formed by teammates; trains narration, justification, and tableau work.
instructions: One or two presenters narrate a slideshow about a suggested trip/event. For each 'click', 2-4 teammates instantly freeze into an unplanned tableau; the presenter must justify whatever they see as the next slide ('Here's the moment Greg discovered the bees'). Run 8-12 slides with escalating narrative. Coach posers: make bold, varied shapes; coach presenters: describe what IS there, then add story.
variations: Expert lecture with diagram tableaux; family photo album.

name: Sound Effects Scene
description: Two players act a scene while two others provide all sound effects vocally; trains offer-reading and audio-physical coordination.
instructions: Two actors take a scene suggestion; two offstage players make every sound effect with their voices (doors, animals, machines). Actors must incorporate and justify every sound, including mistakes; foley players must watch closely and serve the action. Swap roles. Coach: sounds are offers — a surprise dog bark changes the scene; accept it.
variations: Audience members provide sounds; one actor + one foley solo version.

name: Dubbed Movie
description: Two players act in gibberish 'foreign language' while two others dub their voices in English; trains gibberish expressiveness and tight observation.
instructions: Two onstage actors play a scene speaking only gibberish with big physicality and emotional clarity; two offstage dubbers provide synchronized English 'translation' voices. Actors and dubbers co-create: actors leave clear emotional/physical offers; dubbers justify mouth-movement length. Swap roles. Coach gibberish speakers: vary sounds and intonation so the dub has something to ride.
variations: Poet Translator (gibberish poem + grandiose translation); Interpreter interview for pairs.

name: Gibberish Translator
description: Spolin classic: one player speaks pure gibberish; a translator renders it into English; trains communication beyond words and confident interpretation.
instructions: Two players: an Expert who speaks only gibberish, and a Translator. The audience asks the Expert questions (or the host interviews them on a suggested topic). The Expert answers in expressive gibberish — varying melody, tempo, gesture, emotion — and the Translator 'translates', matching the length, tone, and emotional shape of the gibberish. Coach the translator to mirror the gibberish's music; coach the expert to actually communicate intent. Swap roles often.
origin: Viola Spolin, Improvisation for the Theater
variations: Gibberish poetry slam; gibberish sales pitch; solo: argue both sides of a debate in gibberish, then translate yourself.

name: Forward / Reverse
description: A director 'remote controls' a scene, rewinding and fast-forwarding it; players must replay their lines and actions exactly; trains scene memory and precision.
instructions: Two players scene from a suggestion. The director calls 'Reverse!' — players perform their dialogue and movements backwards, line by line — and 'Forward!' to resume, sometimes repeating the same beat several times. Players must recall lines and blocking precisely. Coach: keep blocking crisp so it's rewindable; commit to the same emotional reads each pass.
variations: Add fast-forward (double speed), slow motion, pause, and 'language' buttons.

name: Half Life
description: Replay the same scene in 60, then 30, 15, 7.5 seconds; brutal training in editing, essence-finding, and comic compression.
instructions: Two players improvise a one-minute scene. Then replay the SAME scene in 30 seconds, then 15, then 7, then 3 — keeping the essential beats and biggest laughs while cutting everything else. Coach: identify the scene's spine — the 3-second version is its purest gag. Debrief what survived each halving; that's what mattered.
variations: Double Life (expand 15s to 2min); replay halvings in different genres.

name: Genre Replay
description: The same short scene is replayed in different film/literary genres; trains genre fluency and committed stylistic shifts.
instructions: Two players run a 1-minute mundane scene (returning a library book). Then replay it as: film noir, horror, rom-com, nature documentary, Shakespearean tragedy, telenovela — keeping the same basic events but transforming language, physicality, pacing, and music of speech. Get genre suggestions from the group. Coach: genre lives in specifics (noir = clipped metaphors, shadows, cigarettes), not just accents.
variations: Mid-scene genre dings; solo: retell your morning in three genres aloud.

name: Expert Interview
description: A player is interviewed as the world's leading expert on an absurd topic and must answer everything with total authority; trains confident bullshitting and specificity.
instructions: One interviewer, one expert. The expert receives an absurd specialty (competitive cloud naming; medieval elevator repair). The interviewer asks sincere journalistic questions; the expert answers with complete confidence, concrete details, anecdotes, and jargon — never breaking authority. 5 minutes, then swap. Coach: specificity is everything ('In 1442, the guild ruled...'). Two-headed variant: two players answer as one expert, alternating words.
variations: Word-at-a-time expert; gibberish expert with translator; solo: record yourself answering 5 interview questions as an expert.

name: Character Walks
description: Players walk the room letting different body parts lead, discovering characters from physicality outward; the core physical character-building drill.
instructions: Walk neutrally around the room. The leader names a body part — nose, chest, pelvis, knees, forehead — and you let it lead your walk, exaggerating to 10 then dialing to a playable 5. Notice what person emerges: How old are they? What do they want? Add a voice, a catchphrase, a greeting to others you pass. Hold one character and answer interview questions in it. Build a stable of 5+ characters over repeated sessions.
variations: Lead with emotions instead of body parts; meet other characters and have two-line exchanges; solo at home with a mirror.

name: Animal Work
description: Build a character from an animal's movement and energy, then humanize it; classic acting-school approach to bold characterization.
instructions: Choose an animal. Spend 2-3 minutes moving as the animal literally — spine, tempo, eyes, breath. Gradually stand upright and 'humanize' to 20% animal: the heron becomes a wary, precise accountant; the bulldog a stubborn doorman. Speak as this person; do a simple task (order coffee) in character. In pairs, play a short scene where both characters are humanized animals. Debrief what the animal gave you that thinking wouldn't have.
origin: Stanislavski/drama-school tradition, used in improv character classes
variations: Guess each other's animals; animal status pairs (predator/prey scenes).

name: Exaggeration Circle
description: A small gesture+sound is passed around the circle, each player exaggerating it slightly until it becomes enormous; trains heightening and shamelessness.
instructions: Circle up. Player 1 makes a tiny gesture with a small sound (a sniff, a finger wiggle). Player 2 repeats it 10% bigger. Continue around the circle, each player amplifying, until the final player performs a full-body, full-voice eruption. Start a new seed. Coach: exaggerate the SAME gesture, don't change it; the discipline is fidelity plus amplitude.
variations: Emotion exaggeration; vocal-only version for tonality work.

name: Status Walks
description: Johnstone-derived drill where players embody numbered status levels in posture, eye contact, and speech, then interact; the foundational status-awareness exercise.
instructions: Walk the room as status 1 (minimal eye contact, hesitant steps, touching your face, broken sentences) through status 10 (still head, sustained eye contact, slow full movements, completed sentences). Call numbers to switch. Then card version: everyone draws a playing card and plays that status while mingling at an imaginary party; afterwards, line up in guessed status order and reveal. Debrief specific behaviors: head stillness, 'er' sounds, who breaks eye contact first.
variations: Card on forehead (you see everyone's but your own — treat others by their card, guess your own); play one status point above/below your partner.

name: Status Swap Scene
description: Two players start at opposite status extremes and gradually trade places by the end of the scene; trains dynamic status play, the engine of drama.
instructions: Two players: A starts high status (boss, expert, celebrity), B low (intern, fan, applicant). Play a 3-minute scene during which status flips completely and GRADUALLY — through revelations, mistakes, leverage shifts — so B ends high and A low. No sudden flips; each line should move the see-saw one notch. Debrief the exact moments status moved and what behavior signaled it.
variations: Master/Servant scenes; status played against role (low-status king, high-status beggar).

name: Master and Servant
description: Johnstone scene structure where one player serves and one commands, exploring how status is negotiated through behavior rather than role.
instructions: Two players: a master and a servant, with a simple situation (preparing for a banquet). Round 1: play it straight — servant raises master's status at every turn. Round 2: servant secretly controls everything while maintaining deferential form (the classic 'Jeeves' dynamic). Round 3: master desperately needs the servant's approval. Coach: status is what you DO, not the job title. Note which dynamic generates the most interesting scene.
variations: Master Servant Disaster game (servant must justify increasingly bad news); three-tier chains (master-steward-servant).

name: The Hat Game
description: Two players scene while each secretly tries to gently remove the other's hat; Johnstone's drill for split attention, soft focus, and physical presence.
instructions: Both players wear soft hats and play an ordinary scene. At any moment either may try to take the other's hat — but only with a smooth, unhurried movement (no snatching, no guarding with hands, no leaning away). If your hat is taken, the round ends. The scene must stay primary; the hat attempt should emerge from natural movement. Trains relaxed, wide attention — the state Johnstone considered ideal for improvising.
variations: Hat duel as a pure standalone (no scene); status assigned before the round.

name: What Comes Next?
description: Johnstone narrative drill: performers ask the audience/coach 'What comes next?' before each action, training story obviousness and audience-serving.
instructions: One or two performers begin a story title. Before each beat they ask 'What comes next?' and the audience (or a partner) supplies the next event; performers enact it, then ask again. When suggestions derail, performers may say 'too soon' or pick another, teaching what stories need vs. want. Solo version: ask yourself aloud and answer with the most OBVIOUS next event, never the cleverest. Reveals that audiences crave obvious, well-constructed stories.
variations: Written solo version as a story-outlining drill; group circle where each person answers.

name: Boring Scene Challenge
description: Players are instructed to make the scene as boring as possible; paradoxically removes performance anxiety and produces grounded, truthful scenes.
instructions: Two players are told: 'Make this scene utterly boring. Nothing clever, no jokes, no drama.' They play two people doing a mundane task with mundane talk. Because the pressure to be interesting is gone, players relax, listen, and react honestly — and the scene usually becomes engaging. Debrief: what made it watchable anyway? (Honest reactions, small behavior.) Use as an antidote whenever a group is pushing for laughs.
origin: Keith Johnstone's 'don't be original' teaching; widely used
variations: 'Be average' coaching call mid-scene; compete for the most boring scene.

name: Colombian Hypnosis
description: Boal's classic: one player 'hypnotizes' a partner who must keep their face a fixed distance from the leader's moving hand; trains leading, following, and embodied attention.
instructions: Pairs. A holds a palm 20-40cm from B's face. A moves the hand slowly in all directions and levels; B must keep their face exactly that distance from the palm at all times — crouching, twisting, rising. Lead your partner into positions they never normally take, without endangering them. Swap after 3 minutes. Then try both hands with two followers, or chains where everyone leads someone and follows someone else. Debrief: which felt more natural, leading or following?
origin: Augusto Boal, Games for Actors and Non-Actors
variations: Indian hypnosis (eye-to-eye); whole-group chains; hypnosis while the leader also follows someone.

name: Complete the Image
description: Boal image-theatre drill: partners alternately freeze into tableaux that 'complete' each other's frozen pose; trains instant physical offers and reading of images.
instructions: Pairs. A and B shake hands and freeze. A steps out, observes the image, and re-enters in a NEW pose that gives the remaining frozen B a different meaning (B's outstretched hand becomes a beggar's plea, a salute, a dance invitation). Then B steps out and completes A's pose differently. Alternate without talking or planning for several minutes; speed up. Group version: one image in the center, anyone replaces. Debrief the variety of meanings one body can take.
origin: Augusto Boal, Games for Actors and Non-Actors
variations: Add a line of dialogue from each new pose to seed scenes; themed images (power, family).

name: Glass Cobra
description: Boal trust/sensory game: a blind 'snake' of players disperses and must reassemble by touch alone; builds ensemble sensitivity.
instructions: Players form a single-file line, hands on the shoulders of the person ahead, eyes closed. Each player explores the shoulders/head/neck of the person in front with their hands to memorize them. The leader then disperses everyone around the room (eyes still closed). On the signal, the 'glass cobra' must reassemble in the original order using touch alone. Debrief on attention quality and how recognition felt.
origin: Augusto Boal, Games for Actors and Non-Actors
variations: Pairs version (find your partner's hands in a blind crowd).

name: Mirror
description: Partners mirror each other's movements in real time, progressing until no one is leading; Spolin's flagship connection exercise.
instructions: Pairs face each other. A leads slow movements; B mirrors precisely, as a reflection. Goal: move so connectedly an observer can't tell who leads. Swap leaders on a call. Final stage 'follow the follower': nobody leads — the movement emerges between you. Coach: soft eye contact on the whole person (not the hands), slow tempo, breathe together. 2-3 minutes per stage. Variation: vocal mirror (mirror speech sounds simultaneously).
origin: Viola Spolin, Improvisation for the Theater
variations: Group mirror (circle mirrors one rotating leader); distorting mirror (B exaggerates); speech mirroring for conversation practice.

name: Space Walk
description: Spolin sensory exercise: players walk exploring the air as a tangible unknown substance, then through changing imagined environments; grounds attention in the body and space.
instructions: Walk the room. Side-coach: 'Feel the space around you as a substance — not water or honey, something unknown. Let it touch you; move through it with your whole body, your face, your eyelids.' Then shift environments: walk through deep snow, hot sand, a crowded subway, zero gravity, a forest at night — letting tempo, weight, and posture change. End by walking 'as yourself entering a party' and notice what changed. 10 minutes of full sensory commitment.
origin: Viola Spolin, Improvisation for the Theater
variations: Space walk with emotion shifts; solo daily as a pre-performance grounding ritual.

name: Build a Room
description: Players take turns entering an empty stage and using invisible objects, building a shared detailed environment one object at a time; the core space-object memory drill.
instructions: Define a door. Player 1 enters, uses one invisible object (opens a fridge, takes juice), exits. Player 2 enters, must use Player 1's object accurately (same location, same height/weight) plus add one new object. Continue through the whole group, each player re-using ALL previous objects then adding one. Group polices consistency (fridge door swings the same way). Debrief: object permanence makes imaginary worlds believable.
setup: open space with a defined door
origin: Spolin Where-games lineage; standard class exercise
variations: Two-player speed version; build then play a scene inside the finished room.

name: Twenty Objects
description: Mime twenty different objects in rapid succession; speed prevents overthinking and builds object-work fluency.
instructions: Solo or in front of the group: a timer starts and you must mime handling twenty distinct objects in 2 minutes — establish each with shape, weight, and one use (drink the coffee, swing the bat, thread the needle), then drop it and move on. No repeats. Group calls out the count. Debrief which objects read clearly and why (resistance, weight, specific grips). Repeat weekly; it's a workout, not a performance.
variations: Themed sets (kitchen, toolshed); partner guesses each object; Infinite Box (boxes within boxes).

name: Tug of War
description: Two players (or teams) mime a tug-of-war with an invisible rope; the classic shared-object give-and-take exercise.
instructions: Two players grip an invisible rope and tug. The rope must stay a constant length — when A pulls, B lurches forward. Play to win physically but agree imaginatively: take turns 'losing ground', sell the strain in your whole body and face, and end with one side winning decisively. Team version with four per side requires the whole line to track the same rope. Debrief: you can compete in fiction only by cooperating in reality.
variations: Invisible ball games (catch with changing ball weights); revolving door; shared heavy table lift.

name: Helping Hands
description: One player speaks while a partner standing behind provides their arms and gestures; trains verbal-physical coordination and justification.
instructions: Player A stands with hands behind their back; Player B stands behind, threading their arms through as A's arms. A delivers a monologue, cooking demo, or interview on a suggestion; B gestures, handles (real or mimed) props, scratches A's nose, etc. A must justify and incorporate every gesture; B must listen and serve (or playfully sabotage) the speech. Swap. Coach A: never ignore a gesture — let it change your speech.
variations: Real food/water props for chaos; two helping-hands pairs in one scene.

name: Puppets
description: Two onstage players are physically posed and moved by two 'puppeteers' while voicing the scene themselves; trains justification of imposed physicality.
instructions: Two 'puppet' players stand limp; two puppeteers (from the group or audience) move their limbs, heads, and bodies into positions throughout the scene. Puppets supply all dialogue, justifying every imposed pose within the story. Puppeteers should move puppets during (not just between) lines. Coach puppets: let the pose change your intention, not just your shape.
variations: One puppet one free player; audience members as puppeteers.

name: Sculptor and Clay
description: One player molds a partner into a statue, then statues come alive; trains physical trust, bold shaping, and embodying received offers.
instructions: Pairs: a sculptor and clay. The sculptor poses the clay limb by limb (touch or air-sculpting) into a statue on a theme ('victory', 'Monday morning'). Gallery walk: sculptors view all statues. Then statues come alive for 30 seconds, speaking as the character they were shaped into. Swap roles. Coach clay players: hold poses precisely and let the pose tell you who you are.
origin: Boal image theatre / drama games tradition
variations: Group sculptures; sculptor works blind; statue pairs start a scene together.

name: Family Portraits
description: On a theme, the group instantly arranges into a frozen 'family photo' with strong character choices; trains fast bold characterization and composition.
instructions: Caller announces a family ('circus family', 'family of villains', 'family on a diet') and counts down from 10. The group instantly arranges a posed family photo, each member making a distinct character choice (the proud one, the jealous one, the baby). On 'click', hold; the caller may tap members to speak one line in character. New theme, new portrait, ideally faster each round.
origin: Drama games tradition; used by Canadian Improv Games
variations: Portraits that animate into 30-second scenes; year-by-year aging portraits.

name: Stakes Circle
description: Around a circle, players build a scenario then take turns adding compounding stakes; isolates the skill of making things matter.
instructions: Circle up. Player 1 names a location; Player 2 describes two characters there; Player 3 gives them a problem. Then each subsequent player adds a stake that compounds ('...and the wedding is tomorrow', '...and she never told him about the loan', '...and the train only runs once a week'). Keep stakes personal and specific, not just bigger explosions. When the scenario is bursting, two players play the scene. Repeat.
variations: Solo written version: take any premise and list 10 escalating stakes.

name: Get Them To...
description: Each player receives a secret objective to get their scene partner to do something; trains playing tactics and reading a partner.
instructions: Two players each draw a secret objective ('get them to leave the room', 'get them to apologize', 'get them to hug you'). Play an ordinary scene (roommates, coworkers) while pursuing your objective through tactics — charm, guilt, bargaining — without ever stating it. Scene ends when an objective lands or after 3 minutes. Observers guess the objectives. Debrief which tactics worked, and note this is how objectives drive all scenes.
origin: Acting pedagogy (actioning) adapted to improv; documented at ImprovDr
variations: Both objectives conflict directly; objectives are emotions to induce rather than actions.

name: Finding the Game (If-Then)
aliases: If This Is True Then What Else
description: The core UCB scene-comedy drill: establish a normal base reality, spot the first unusual thing, then repeatedly ask 'if that's true, what else is true?' to heighten a pattern.
instructions: Two players start a grounded everyday scene and 'yes-and' until something slightly off appears (the first unusual thing). Name and agree on it, then stop adding new ideas: instead ask 'if this unusual thing is true, then what ELSE would be true?' and produce a second example, a third, a fourth — each a bigger logical consequence of the same premise, not a new joke. Ground each heighten in why your character cares. Coach: explore one game fully rather than piling on unrelated bits.
origin: UCB Comedy Improvisation Manual (Besser, Roberts, Walsh)
variations: Coach freezes the scene the instant the first unusual thing appears and asks the group to brainstorm 5 'if-then' heightens before resuming; emotional-game version where the pattern is an escalating feeling.

name: Why Do You Do That?
description: Players explore an established scene game by asking each other 'why do you do that?', justifying odd behavior emotionally instead of inventing new oddities.
instructions: Run a scene until one character does something unusual. The partner asks, sincerely and in character, 'Why do you do that?' The first player answers with an emotionally true reason, which deepens the pattern. Keep asking 'why' and 'what does that feel like' to explore the same behavior rather than topic-hopping. Coach: exploration beats invention — mine one idea for everything it's worth.
origin: Will Hines / UCB pedagogy ('Heighten and Explore')
variations: Coach calls 'explore!' to force three more details about the current behavior before any new idea is allowed.

name: Goal and Obstacles
description: Circle game alternating an obstacle ('unfortunately...') and a yes-and solution ('fortunately...'); trains positivity, problem-solving, and narrative momentum.
instructions: Stand in a circle. Player 1 states a goal ('I'm going to bake a cake'). Player 2 says 'Unfortunately...' and adds an obstacle ('...the oven is broken'). Player 3 says 'Fortunately...' or 'Yes, and...' and overcomes it ('...I found a campfire'). Continue around the circle, alternating obstacle and solution, keeping one story alive to a triumphant or absurd end. Coach: solutions should accept the obstacle's reality, not erase it.
variations: Pure 'Fortunately/Unfortunately' alternation with no solving; pairs version building one tall tale.

name: Sound Ball
description: Players throw an imaginary ball across a circle, each throw paired with a vocal sound (and the catcher echoing it); trains vocal spontaneity and committed offers.
instructions: Circle up. Mime throwing a ball to someone across the circle while making any vocal sound ('Bwaaap!'). The catcher receives the ball by repeating that exact sound, then turns and throws to a new person with a brand-new sound of their own. Keep eye contact and full commitment; no real words allowed. Add a second ball/sound for chaos. Coach: don't pre-plan the sound — let it fly out on the throw.
origin: Spolin-derived warmup; standard at most schools
variations: Sound-and-motion ball (add a gesture the catcher copies); transform the sound as you pass it on; emotion ball where each throw carries a feeling.

name: Red Ball
description: An imaginary 'red ball' is passed by name around a circle, with more named objects added until several are in play at once; trains focus, naming clarity, and tracking multiple offers.
instructions: Circle up. Hold up an imaginary object, make eye contact, say 'Red ball' and mime tossing it; the receiver must say 'Red ball?' (confirm) — 'Red ball!' (sender) — then pass it on, always re-naming. Once it flows, introduce a second object ('A sleeping baby'), then a third ('An angry cat'), each tracked and named on every pass. Things break down hilariously; that's the point. Coach: confirm before you throw, and keep each object's handling consistent (the baby is gentle, the cat thrashes).
variations: Pass 4 (four distinct objects circulating at once); transform each object into something else when you receive it.

name: Transformation of Objects
description: An imaginary object is passed around a circle, each player transforming it into something new through how they handle it; trains object work and seeing offers in shapes.
instructions: Player 1 mimes using an object (a broom — sweeping). They pass it to Player 2, who handles the same imaginary shape but lets it become something new through use (the broom becomes a guitar, then a fishing rod, then a baby). No naming aloud — the transformation must read physically. Go around the circle; objects should change radically by the end. Coach: let the object's weight and shape suggest the next thing; don't decide before you receive it.
variations: Players name what they made after using it; partner-guess version.

name: Loser Ball
description: A ball-toss circle with the rule that no one may successfully catch the ball and everyone must celebrate the failure; trains embracing mistakes and supporting each other.
instructions: Circle up with an imaginary ball. Two rules: (1) no one is allowed to actually 'catch' it — you must fumble, drop, or miss it; (2) the whole group energetically supports and celebrates each failed catch ('Ohhh!' / cheering). Pass it around so everyone fails gloriously and gets applauded. Debrief: what changed when failure was the goal? Use whenever a group fears mistakes.
variations: Failure Bow circle: each player makes a deliberate 'mistake' and takes a triumphant bow while the group cheers.

name: Murder Chain
description: A player must silently communicate a location, an occupation, and an object to a partner through mime alone within a time limit; trains clear physical storytelling.
instructions: Player 1 receives three things from the group: a location, an occupation, and an object (e.g., aquarium / accountant / chainsaw). With no words, they have one minute to make Player 2 understand all three through object work and behavior. Player 2 guesses aloud as clues land. Swap and repeat with new combinations. Coach: establish space first, then occupation through activity, then introduce the object distinctly.
variations: Whole-group charades-style guessing; add an emotion as a fourth item.

name: Breaking Routines
description: A solo player establishes a precise activity routine, then repeats it with two interruptions — one minor, one catastrophic; trains object permanence and physical reaction.
instructions: Solo. Build a detailed routine with imaginary objects (make coffee: grind, pour, stir, sip) so the audience knows the space. Repeat the exact routine, but this time introduce a minor break (you're out of milk) and respond truthfully, then a catastrophic break (the kettle explodes) and respond fully. Coach: the routine must be established faithfully first or the breaks mean nothing; let your body react before your words.
variations: Pair version where a partner causes the breaks; build the whole thing into a wordless one-person scene.

name: Fix a Problem, Leave a Problem
description: Players pass through a shared location one at a time, each fixing one problem and creating a new one; trains environment work and consequence.
instructions: Establish a location with a defined entrance (a messy kitchen). Players enter one at a time. Each player must FIX one existing problem (mop the spill) and LEAVE one new problem (knock over the flour), all through object work, then exit. The next player must notice the new problem and fix it while adding their own. Continue through the whole group; the room's history accumulates. Coach: react to what the last person left before adding yours.
setup: open space with a defined door
variations: Two-player tag version; verbal-only version (fix one fact, introduce one complication).

name: Parallel Initiations
description: Two players begin a scene simultaneously, each absorbed in a different activity, then must weave a relationship and reality between them; trains initiating from behavior and connecting unrelated offers.
instructions: Each player privately picks a different physical activity (one folds laundry, one tunes a guitar). On 'go', both start their activity at the same time without consulting. After 15-20 seconds of parallel work, they begin to relate — who are these two people sharing a space, and how do these activities connect? Build a grounded scene from there. Coach: don't drop your activity the instant you speak; let the two realities inform a single one.
variations: Three-player triangle version; coach assigns the two activities to force odd combinations.

name: Trapped
description: A solo player mimes escaping a small contained environment (bear trap, stuck elevator, straitjacket); trains detailed object work and physical problem-solving under pressure.
instructions: Solo. Choose a small, contained predicament — foot in a bear trap, stuck in an elevator, tangled in a hammock, locked in a phone booth. Establish the environment's exact dimensions and resistances through mime, then physically problem-solve your way out in real time, reacting to each failed attempt. Coach: keep the boundaries consistent (the elevator walls don't move); let frustration and small victories show.
variations: Add narration; pair version where one is trapped and one tries to help (badly).

name: The Where Game
description: One player silently establishes a location through object work; others enter only once they believe they know where it is; trains wordless environment-building and reading of space.
instructions: Player 1 picks a location secretly and begins using objects that reveal it (stamping passports, checking a watch, scanning a board — an airport gate). When any watching player thinks they know the Where, they enter and join the activity, behaving consistently with that location — but NOT naming it. Players keep entering as they catch on. Coach: reveal the place through specific objects and behavior, never by announcing it; if you enter wrong, justify and adapt.
variations: Specialized Where (mash two locations: swamp office, space classroom); audience guesses the location at the end.

name: Rhyme Ball
description: Solo musical-improv drill: pick a word and rattle off as many rhymes as possible without stopping; builds the rhyming reflex needed for improvised songs.
instructions: Pick any word (or name an object you can see). Out loud, rapidly list every word that rhymes with it — real, slant, or near rhymes — without pausing to judge. When your brain slows, switch to a new word and go again. Do 5 minutes daily. Coach: speed and volume of attempts matter far more than cleverness; near-rhymes count. Progress to rhyming whole phrases.
origin: Musical improv pedagogy (Bay Area Musical Improv and others)
variations: Group 'rhyme ball' tossing a word around a circle for rhymes; rhyme on a deadline (one rhyme per beat of a metronome).

name: Rhyming Couplets Circle
description: Group musical drill where each player sings a rhyming couplet describing a shared location or topic; trains singing within rhythm and on-the-spot rhyme.
instructions: Pick a location or topic and a simple melody (or accompaniment). Going around the circle, each player sings one rhyming couplet about the topic that fits the melody and tempo (line A sets up, line B rhymes and lands). Stay in rhythm above all — finishing on the beat matters more than a perfect rhyme. Pass cleanly to the next singer. Coach: leave your rhyme word for the END of the line so your brain has time.
variations: Blues structure (chorus hook + verses of two couplets); ABAB quatrains; group writes one verse line each plus a shared chorus.

name: Diddly Dum
