description: A short sung/spoken rhythmic phrase ('diddly dum') is passed and varied around a circle; trains rhythm, focus, and confident vocal passing for musical improv.
instructions: Circle up. One player sings or chants a short rhythmic nonsense phrase ('diddly-diddly-dum') with a clear pulse. The next player repeats it back, then either passes the same phrase on or offers a slight variation. Keep a steady group tempo; the phrase travels around, mutating gently. Use as a calming, focusing musical warmup before songs. Coach: lock to the pulse before you embellish.
variations: Add pitch (sung not chanted); call-and-response where the group answers each phrase.

name: Sing to a Track
description: Solo drill: improvise sung lyrics and melody over a pre-recorded instrumental; builds the ability to invent words and tune while riding accompaniment.
instructions: Find an instrumental backing track (e.g. 'unfinished songs' style tracks online). Play it and improvise a complete song on a chosen topic — verse, chorus, bridge — making up melody and lyrics in real time, landing phrases on the chord changes. Don't stop when you fumble; sing through it. Record and review. Coach: let the music tell you when to start and stop phrases; rhyme on downbeats.
variations: Harmonize over recorded songs using the 1-3-5 method; sing the plot of a movie you just watched.

name: Typewriter
description: One player narrates a story aloud like an author at a typewriter while teammates act out everything the narrator describes, including dialogue tags they must then speak.
instructions: One player is the Author, seated, narrating an original story ('She crept into the abandoned mill, certain she was alone...'). The rest enact exactly what's narrated, in real time. When the Author writes a line of dialogue ('...and she whispered:'), the relevant actor must instantly supply that line. Actors can prompt the Author by doing something the Author then 'writes'. Coach: Author paints vivid, performable images; actors commit to every word, even awkward ones.
variations: Multiple authors trading off; actors-only stretches where the Author goes silent and the scene self-narrates.

name: Backwards Scene
description: Players construct an entire scene in reverse, starting from its ending and working back to the opening line; trains causality awareness and reverse-engineering story.
instructions: Two players are given (or invent) the final image/line of a scene — e.g. one storming out shouting 'I never want to see you again!' They play that ending first, then perform the beat that came just before it, then the one before that, working backwards to the scene's calm opening. Each earlier beat must logically produce the later one you just played. Coach: keep emotional continuity intact; the audience should be able to mentally play it forward.
variations: Whole story told in reverse chapters; alternate forwards/backwards on a director's call.

name: Inner Voices
description: Two players run a scene while two teammates voice each character's private inner thoughts; trains subtext awareness and the gap between thought and speech.
instructions: Two players play a scene (a tense first date, a job review). Behind or beside each, a teammate speaks that character's unspoken inner monologue out loud after each line ('She thinks: don't mention the ex, do NOT mention the ex'). The scene players react to their own inner voice — it can contradict what they say. Coach: inner voices reveal real wants; let the contrast create comedy and honesty.
variations: Solo version: speak your own character's spoken line then its inner-voice contradiction; 'devil and angel' two inner voices per character.

name: Evil Twin
description: A 'twin' tags in to make a wild or destructive choice that the original player must justify when they return; trains justification and commitment to bold offers.
instructions: Two players run a scene; a third stands by as the 'evil twin' of one of them. At any point the evil twin taps the original out, takes their exact place, and does/says something bold, rude, or chaotic ('I quit and I'm taking the dog'), then taps back out. The original player returns and must justify whatever the twin just did as if they'd done it. Coach: the twin makes the choice the scene was too polite to make; the original owns it fully.
variations: Twin makes only positive over-the-top choices; both players have twins.

name: Entrances and Exits
description: Each player is secretly assigned a trigger word; whenever it's spoken they must justify entering or leaving the stage; trains active justification and scene flexibility.
instructions: Each player gets a secret trigger (a common word, a number, or a phrase). A scene begins. Whenever a player's onstage trigger is spoken by anyone, that player must immediately find a reason to exit; whenever their offstage trigger is spoken, they must enter and justify it. The scene continually reshuffles its cast and must stay coherent. Coach: justify every entrance/exit inside the story, never mechanically.
variations: One trigger per player that flips them between two characters; audience-supplied trigger words.

name: Sounds Like a Song
description: A director listens for a 'song-worthy' line in a scene and calls 'Sounds like a song!', cueing that player to break into an improvised song built on the line.
instructions: Run any scene. A side-coach/director listens for a line that could anchor a song and shouts 'Sounds like a song about [that]!' The player who said it must immediately launch into a short improvised song using that line as the title/hook, while others may join as backing singers, then the scene resumes. Coach: repeat the hook line as your chorus to buy thinking time; keep verses on-topic.
variations: Genre assigned for each song; group hoedown where everyone adds a verse in turn.

name: Word Machine
description: A teammate supplies a random word on tap that scene players must instantly weave in and justify; trains incorporating randomness without derailing.
instructions: Two players run a scene. A designated 'word machine' (a teammate, or audience) calls out a random word whenever tapped or at intervals. The next thing a player says must include and justify that word naturally ('...which is exactly why I keep a FERRET in the glovebox'). The scene must continue making sense. Coach: don't comment on the weird word — absorb it as if it always belonged.
variations: Solo: open a book, point to random words, work each into a monologue; words drawn from audience.

name: Moving People
description: Scene players may not move themselves at all; teammates or audience members physically pose them throughout the scene; trains vocal justification of imposed physicality.
instructions: Two players play a scene but are forbidden to move any part of their own bodies. Volunteers (teammates or audience) move their arms, heads, and whole bodies into positions and walk them around the stage. The scene players supply all dialogue and must justify every pose and move ('Oh, I see you want me to kneel... fine, I'll propose'). Coach: react to where your body lands as if you chose it.
origin: Whose Line ('Moving People') / Canadian Improv Games
variations: Only one player is moved; movers cannot touch, only gesture commands.

name: Expand and Advance
description: A director calls 'Expand' to make players dwell and add detail to the current moment, or 'Advance' to skip the story forward; trains pacing control and finding richness vs. momentum.
instructions: Two players run a scene. A director periodically calls 'Expand!' — players slow down and deepen the present beat (more sensory detail, more emotion, more exploration of the current idea) — or 'Advance!' — players jump the story to its next significant beat, skipping the boring connective tissue. Alternate the calls to find the scene's natural rhythm. Coach: 'expand' is not stalling and 'advance' is not rushing; both must serve the story.
origin: Canadian Improv Games / Keith Johnstone lineage
variations: Players self-call expand/advance; 'cut to' film-editing version.

name: Three Rules
description: Each player is given a private behavioral rule that governs their whole scene; trains commitment to a constraint while staying truthful, plus the audience guesses the rules.
instructions: Privately assign each player a rule ('you must agree with everything', 'you can only speak in questions', 'you compliment then insult', 'you mirror your partner's posture'). Play a normal scene; each player obeys their rule throughout without revealing it. At the end the audience guesses each rule. Coach: integrate the rule so it looks like character, not a gimmick.
variations: One shared rule for the whole cast; rules that conflict between partners.

name: Pick Up Stakes
description: Players draw pre-written 'stakes' lines from slips and inject them into a scene to raise tension; trains escalating consequence and justification.
instructions: Pre-write slips with high-stakes revelations ('You're being audited tomorrow', 'I'm pregnant', 'The building is on fire'). Two players begin an ordinary scene; at intervals a player draws and reads a slip as their next line, and both must absorb and escalate from that new stake. Continue drawing as the scene compounds. Coach: react to each stake emotionally before plot-solving; let stakes change the relationship.
variations: Solo written version: list ten escalating stakes for any premise; verbal-only with no slips.

name: More Specific
description: A director repeatedly calls 'More specific!' forcing players to replace vague offers with precise, vivid detail; trains specificity, the engine of believable scenes.
instructions: Run a scene. Whenever a player makes a vague offer ('I got you a gift', 'we should go somewhere'), the director calls 'More specific!' and the player must instantly restate it with concrete detail ('I got you a 1987 Swiss Army knife with your initials engraved'). Call it several times in a row to push past the first easy detail. Coach: specificity creates reality and comedy; names, brands, dates, textures.
origin: Canadian Improv Games / general improv pedagogy
variations: Solo: describe an object, then re-describe it three times more specifically; pair drill where every noun must be specified.

name: Scene Three Ways
description: A neutral scene is replayed twice more, each take recolored by a new style, genre, emotion, or constraint; trains range and the discipline of repeating beats faithfully.
instructions: Two players run a short neutral scene (returning a sweater). Then replay the SAME beats and lines colored by a first style (e.g. silent-film), then again by a second (e.g. opera, or 'everyone is exhausted', or 'set on the moon'). Keep the underlying events identical; only the coloring changes. Coach: the spine stays the same so the audience can feel how style transforms identical content.
variations: Audience picks each style; emotion-only colors; speed changes as the third take.

name: Object Game
description: Players build a scene around a single audience-suggested object that may or may not be used for its real purpose; trains endowment and inventive reframing.
instructions: Get one object (real or named) from the audience — a broom, a stapler. Two players play a scene where the object is central, and it may become anything ('this isn't a broom, it's the last paddle off the sinking ship'). Endow it, re-endow it, and let it drive the relationship and plot. Coach: commit to whatever you decide it is; let the partner's use redefine it.
variations: Prop-bag round where many odd props get reinvented; the object changes meaning every time it's picked up.

name: Circle Gibberish
description: A group 'converses' entirely in gibberish driven by emotion, passing and transforming feelings around the circle; trains emotional expressiveness and reading tone over words.
instructions: Stand in a circle. One player addresses a neighbor in gibberish loaded with a clear emotion (delighted, suspicious, heartbroken). The neighbor reacts in gibberish, then turns and passes a NEW emotion to the next person, who catches and transforms it. Keep gestures and faces fully engaged as if the gibberish means something specific. Coach: commit to intent — you should be able to feel the 'conversation' even without words.
variations: Two-player gibberish argument where each must mirror then top the other's emotion; whole-group gibberish dinner party.

name: Emotional Carpool
description: Players 'drive' together and adopt the strong shared emotion of each new passenger who gets in; trains emotional matching and the comfort of just being emotional together.
instructions: Set up chairs as a car; a driver picks up passengers one at a time. Each new passenger enters with a strong distinct emotion and everyone already in the car gradually catches and matches it (not the cause — just the feeling). When the car is full, the driver drops everyone and the cycle restarts with a new passenger leading. Coach: don't justify or explain the emotion; agree to feel it together and enjoy it.
variations: Hitchhiker emotion version; elevator instead of car with floors as emotion changes.

name: Weather Report
description: A news weather presenter narrates an absurd forecast while teammates embody the conditions; trains confident presentational speaking and vivid description on the fly.
instructions: One player is the weather anchor at a map; a director points to regions as the anchor delivers a lively forecast ('A front of raining cats and dogs sweeps in from the Rockies...'). Teammates physically become the weather (clouds, storms, sunshine) on cue. The anchor must keep professional broadcast energy and specificity while incorporating whatever the 'weather' does. Coach: commit to broadcaster cadence and made-up meteorology jargon.
variations: Full TV News (anchor, field reporter, commercials); sports commentary version.

name: Tag-Team Monologue
description: A solo character delivers a monologue; teammates tag the speaker out and continue the SAME monologue seamlessly as the same character; trains group mind and shared point of view.
instructions: One player begins a monologue as a specific character on a suggested topic ('the day I quit my job'). At any point a waiting player taps them out, takes their place, and continues the exact monologue as that same character, picking up mid-thought and matching voice and viewpoint. Keep tagging so several players voice one continuous person. Coach: it's one character, not a relay of new ones — honor the established details and energy.
origin: iO / long-form opening tradition; documented at ImprovDr
variations: Tag-team song; each tagged player must add one new detail before continuing.

name: String of Pearls
description: A line of players each supply one connecting sentence between a fixed first line and last line, building a complete story bead by bead; trains causal connection and reincorporation.
instructions: 8-12 players stand in a line facing the audience. One volunteer steps forward and says the story's FIRST sentence; another steps to the far end and says the LAST sentence. Then players step forward one at a time, anywhere in the line, each adding a single sentence that helps connect beginning to end, until the whole story makes sense in sequence. Coach: each sentence must bridge logically; later players reincorporate earlier beads.
variations: Pop-Up Storybook (each pearl is a frozen illustrated tableau); fill the gaps in random order then read it back.

name: Beginning, Middle, End
description: Players rapidly deliver complete three-part stories — one sentence each for beginning, middle, and end — often as a relay; trains instant story shape.
instructions: In a circle or trios, players tell complete stories in three sentences: one establishes a normal situation, one introduces a complication, one resolves it. In the relay version, three different players each speak one part of the same story before passing to the next trio. Go fast, several rounds. Coach: the middle must break the beginning's routine; the end must answer the middle.
variations: Six Episodes (expand each into a played scene); add a title drawn from the group.

name: Panel of Experts
description: A panel of self-proclaimed experts on an absurd topic fields audience questions, each answering with total authority; trains confident bluffing and building on co-panelists.
instructions: Three or more players sit as a panel of world experts on a suggested (often ridiculous) subject — 'the science of hiccups', 'medieval emoji'. A moderator takes audience questions; experts answer in turn with confident jargon, statistics, and anecdotes, agreeing with and building on each other ('Yes, and as Dr. Patel's 1987 study showed...'). Coach: never break authority; specificity sells it.
variations: Good/Bad/Ugly advice panel; one panelist is secretly clueless.

name: Good, Bad, and Worse Advice
aliases: The Good the Bad and the Ugly
description: Three advisers answer the same audience problem — one with good advice, one with terrible advice, one with bizarre/absurd advice; trains rapid contrasting perspectives.
instructions: Three players sit as advice-givers, assigned roles: Good (genuinely helpful), Bad (actively harmful but confident), and Worse/Ugly (surreal, off-the-wall). The host reads a real audience dilemma; each adviser answers in turn in their lane, then the host asks a follow-up. Rotate problems. Coach: commit to your lane — the Good answer should actually be good; contrast is the comedy.
variations: Solo: answer one dilemma three ways yourself; add a fourth 'devil's advocate' adviser.

name: Reruns
description: The same short scene is replayed several times, each pass recolored by a new emotion or tone called by the audience; trains emotional range and faithful repetition.
instructions: Two players run a short neutral scene. Then replay the exact same scene (same events and roughly the same lines) under a new emotional tone each time — first furious, then giddy, then grief-stricken, then seductive. Get the emotions from the audience. Coach: keep the bones identical so the audience can feel how emotion alone transforms the same content.
variations: Genre reruns instead of emotions; dial intensity 1-10 across passes.

name: Naive Expert
description: A player is interviewed as an authority but knows nothing, blustering through questions while a partner feeds confidence; trains commitment over correctness.
instructions: One player is an 'expert' on a topic they have no information about; an interviewer asks earnest questions. The expert must answer with total confidence, inventing or hilariously dodging, never admitting ignorance ('Great question — the short answer is yes, the long answer is also yes'). Optionally a co-host bails them out. Coach: confidence and commitment to nonsense beat any clever true answer.
variations: Two-headed naive expert answering as one; the topic is revealed to the expert only mid-interview.

name: Hey, Taxi!
description: A cab driver picks up a series of strongly-characterized passengers and gradually mimics each one's traits; trains observation and quick character adoption.
instructions: A player sits as a taxi driver. Passengers (with bold physical/vocal characters, often suggested by the audience) get in one at a time, stating a destination. Within the ride, the driver subtly catches and adopts the current passenger's mannerisms. When that passenger leaves, a new one boards and the driver shifts to their trait. Coach: catch traits organically through conversation, not as a sudden switch.
variations: Passengers' emotions instead of mannerisms; rideshare with multiple passengers at once.

name: The Phone Call (Solo)
description: A solo player performs one side of a phone conversation, making the unheard other person and the relationship fully clear; trains implication, reaction, and listening 'gaps'.
instructions: Solo. Mime answering a phone and conduct an entire conversation playing only your side, leaving realistic pauses for the (invisible) other person. Through your reactions, repeats ('You did WHAT?'), and tone, make it obvious who you're talking to and what they're saying. Build to a clear turn or revelation. Coach: the silences must be active — you're listening to specific things; let them change your face.
variations: Stage version inviting an audience member's real relationships as content; argue with a customer-service line.

name: Monoscene (Solo)
description: A solo improviser plays a full multi-character scene alone by 'ghosting' — switching position, voice, and physicality to embody each character; trains characterization and spatial discipline.
instructions: Solo. Pick a situation with 2-3 characters (a tense dinner, a job interview). Assign each character a fixed spot on stage, a distinct voice, and posture. Play the scene by physically moving to each character's spot and shifting fully into them to deliver their lines, leaving clear beats so the audience tracks who's who. Keep the topography consistent. Coach: change BODY and VOICE, not just the spot; let characters react to each other.
variations: Talk-show format (host + guests); play people you know well; record and review which characters read clearly.

name: Endow and Heighten Lay-Ups
description: Two players initiate simultaneously from opposite sides, each with a clear emotional take on themselves and on their partner, then heighten those feelings back and forth; trains emotional scene initiation.
instructions: Two players stand on opposite sides of the stage. Each privately decides how they FEEL about themselves ('I'm thrilled') and about their partner ('I'm wary of you'). On 'go', both initiate at once from those feelings and then heighten — each line ramps the emotion in response to the other — until the coach calls scene. Coach: lead with feeling, not plot; let the two emotions collide and grow.
origin: iO / UCB emotional scene pedagogy (Improv Does Best)
variations: Mirrored emotions (both same feeling), complementary, or opposite; personal vs scenic emphasis rounds.

name: The Great Game of Power
description: Boal exercise using a table and chairs: players arrange the objects to depict the most powerful possible configuration, then place themselves to dominate; trains status and spatial power literacy.
instructions: Set out a table, five chairs, and a bottle. One at a time, players rearrange the objects to make ONE chair the most powerful element in the picture (no breaking/destroying allowed); the group discusses each arrangement. Next phase: a player takes a position of power among the objects without moving them; others enter one at a time, each trying to place themselves in an even MORE powerful position relative to the rest. Debrief what reads as power: height, centrality, distance, orientation.
setup: a table, several chairs, a bottle
origin: Augusto Boal, Games for Actors and Non-Actors
variations: Add dialogue once positions are set; freeze and ask the audience who has the power and why.

name: Half-Life Musical
description: An improvised song is replayed in successively halved durations; trains finding a song's essential hook and compressing musical ideas.
instructions: Players improvise a full song on a suggestion (about 60 seconds). Then perform the SAME song in 30 seconds, then 15, then 8, keeping the central hook and biggest musical moment while cutting verses and filler. Each pass forces you to identify what the song is really 'about'. Coach: the chorus/hook usually survives to the end — that's the song's spine.
variations: Double Life expanding a 10-second song to two minutes; halve in different genres.

name: Broccoli Cauliflower
description: Two players hold an entire emotional conversation using only one fixed word each ('broccoli' vs 'cauliflower'); trains conveying meaning through tone, rhythm, and body alone.
instructions: Two players are each assigned a single word. They must hold a complete scene — an argument, a flirtation, a negotiation — saying ONLY their word, varying pitch, volume, pace, and gesture to carry all meaning. After 2-3 minutes, the pair tells the group what the conversation was 'about'; the group guesses. Coach: subtext lives entirely in delivery here, exactly as in real talk.
variations: Use numbers instead of words; gibberish version; the two words must be opposites.

name: Bus Stop
description: Players wait at and board a bus, each portraying a destination, mood, or character purely through body language; trains physical characterization and silent storytelling.
instructions: Set a bench as a bus stop. Players approach and wait, each silently embodying a clear character with a destination and emotional state (late for a funeral, off to a first date). As an imaginary bus arrives, each boards in character. Observers guess each person's situation. Coach: tell the whole story with posture, tempo, and the way you scan for the bus — no words needed.
variations: Add one line each as they board; weather affects everyone's body (Bus Trip in a storm).

name: Emotional Symphony
description: A conductor assigns each player an emotion and cues their volume/intensity like an orchestra; trains instant emotional access and gradation.
instructions: Players stand in a line; each is assigned a distinct emotion (a gibberish or single-phrase 'instrument' expressing it). A conductor points to bring players 'in' and uses height of hand to set intensity, building solos, duets, and full-ensemble crescendos of pure emotion. Coach players to find real gradations (a whisper of grief vs. a wail) and to start/stop crisply on cue.
variations: Words/sentences instead of sounds; audience supplies emotions; sound-only soundscape version.

name: Pillars
description: Two players run a scene and, whenever they pause, tap a 'pillar' (another player) who supplies the next word, which they must justify; trains justification and incorporating randomness.
instructions: Two volunteers stand at the front corners as 'pillars'. Two players play a scene; whenever a player reaches a natural gap or deliberately trails off mid-sentence, they touch a pillar, who instantly supplies a word. The player must say that word as their next word and justify it within the scene, continuing fluidly. Coach: trail off ON a word that needs help; never reject the pillar's offer.
variations: Pillars-Faces (pillar makes a face the player justifies); pillars supply whole phrases for advanced players.

name: La Ronde
description: A chain of two-person scenes where one character carries over into the next scene with a new partner; trains character consistency across contexts and seamless transitions.
instructions: A and B play a scene. At the switch, A exits and B stays, joined by new player C for a fresh scene — B is the SAME character in a new situation. Then B exits, C continues with D, and so on down the chain, each character appearing in exactly two consecutive scenes. The final scene loops back to the first character to close the ring. Coach: keep each carried-over character utterly consistent even as the world around them changes.
origin: Long-form format after Schnitzler's play; iO/People and Chairs
variations: Themed La Ronde (all scenes about secrets); status La Ronde where each handoff flips status.

name: Restaurant
description: Audience members sit as diners with a theme; players rotate in as waiters/staff who each do something fitting the theme; trains theme-running and quick character entrances.
instructions: Two volunteers sit as restaurant patrons; get a theme (e.g. 'everything is a euphemism', 'the world's worst service'). Players enter one at a time as servers, chefs, or other staff, each performing a distinct bit that fits the theme, interacting with the diners, then exiting to let the next staff member enter. Coach: each entrance is a new clear character with one strong choice; heighten the theme each time.
variations: Restaurant Quirks (each server has a secret quirk the diners guess); two competing tables.

name: Da Doo Ron Ron
description: Group rhyming song game to the tune of the 1960s hit; players take turns adding rhyming lines, with elimination when you can't rhyme in time; trains rhyme under pressure and rhythm.
instructions: Stand in a line. To the tune of 'Da Doo Ron Ron', the group sings the refrain ('Da doo ron ron ron, da doo ron ron') between contributions. Starting stage-right, Player 1 sings a setup line; the group refrains; Player 2 adds a rhyming line; refrain; Player 3 must supply three quick rhymes in the fast section. Anyone who fails to rhyme on the beat is eliminated (with a cheer). Continue down the line. Coach: keep the pulse; near-rhymes are fine if they land on time.
variations: Non-elimination practice version; themed rhymes from an audience suggestion.

name: Irish Drinking Song
description: Players build a verse-by-verse song to a simple Irish-pub melody, one line each, on an audience topic; trains rhyme, rhythm, and group song structure with built-in safety.
instructions: Four (or more) players stand in a line. To a repetitive Irish-sounding tune, each sings one line of the song about the given topic, going down the line; four lines complete a verse (with the last line often rhyming or a shared refrain). The next verse starts with the next player. The simple recurring melody and group 'hey!' between verses give thinking time. Coach: leave rhyme words to line-ends; lean on the refrain when stuck.
variations: Blues jam version; sea-shanty melody; add a tragic death in the final verse.

name: Superheroes
description: A hero with an audience-given absurd name tackles a crisis, summoning teammates who each get named by the previous player and must embody that power; trains endowment and yes-anding wild names.
instructions: Get a crisis and a silly superhero name from the audience. The first hero enters narrating the emergency, then calls for help using a made-up name for the next player ('I need you, Captain Mild Inconvenience!'). That player enters and must immediately justify and embody whatever power that name implies, then later summons the next hero with a new name. Build a team that resolves the crisis. Coach: accept your name with delight and define the power through action.
variations: Each hero must out-do the last hero's power; villain-team version.

name: Dating Game
description: A contestant questions three hidden-quirk 'bachelors' on a dating show and tries to guess each one's secret identity; trains indirect character clues and playing-to-guess.
instructions: One player is the contestant and leaves earshot; three players each get a secret quirk or identity (a vampire afraid of commitment; someone who experiences everything in reverse). The contestant returns as the dating-show host and asks the panel romantic questions; each answers in character, leaking clues without stating the quirk. The contestant guesses each quirk and 'picks' a date. Coach panelists: escalate clue obviousness; host: ask questions that expose the quirks.
variations: Job-interview version; the contestant also has a secret quirk.

name: Rashomon
description: A neutral base scene is replayed several times, each time told from a different character's biased point of view; trains perspective, exaggeration, and consistent reincorporation.
instructions: Play a 'neutral' base scene involving several characters from an audience suggestion (an argument at a wedding). Then replay the same events from one character's subjective viewpoint — they're the hero, others are villains or fools — distorting and exaggerating to match their bias. Replay again from another character's POV. Keep the core events fixed; only the slant changes. Coach: each version reveals character through how reality gets bent.
variations: Two POVs side by side (split screen); add narration of each character's inner justification.

name: Pecking Order
description: Each player secretly picks a status number and plays it in a group scene, then everyone lines up in guessed order; trains relative status calibration and reading others.
instructions: Each player in the scene secretly chooses a status number from 1 (highest) to the number of players (doubles allowed). Play a group scene (a staff meeting) where each player behaves at their chosen status relative to everyone else — without knowing others' numbers, so they must calibrate live. After the scene, players guess and arrange themselves in status order, then reveal. Debrief mismatches: where did your status read wrong?
origin: Keith Johnstone status lineage; Improv Encyclopedia
variations: Status ladder (everyone must end in a clear pecking order); animal pecking order in a barnyard.

name: Status Battle
description: Two players compete to claim the highest (or lowest) status in a scene, each move topping the other; trains active status tactics and one-upmanship.
instructions: Two players, a simple setting (a party, a waiting room). Both try to be the HIGHEST-status person present, each line and action subtly putting themselves above the other (name-drops, mild put-downs, taking space). The status see-saws as each tops the last. Run a second round competing for LOWEST status (over-apologizing, self-deprecating). Coach: status is behavior — what you do with your eyes, body, and space, not just words.
variations: Lowest-status battle; play one point above/below your partner at all times.

name: Stunt Double
description: Whenever a scene calls for something difficult, dangerous, or embarrassing, a teammate jumps in as a 'stunt double' to perform it (often in slow motion); trains tag-in timing and physical comedy.
instructions: Two players run a scene. When something hard, dangerous, or awkward is about to happen (a fall, a fight, an intimate moment), a player calls 'Stunt double!' A waiting player swaps in for the relevant actor, performs the action (commonly in exaggerated slow motion), then the original swaps back to continue. Coach: call the double the instant the difficult moment arrives; doubles commit fully and physically.
variations: Emotion double (someone voices the feeling the actor can't); singing double for musical moments.

name: Pan Left, Pan Right
description: Three simultaneous two-person scenes share players; on 'Pan left/right' the lineup shifts so a different pair faces front and continues their scene; trains scene memory and instant re-entry.
instructions: Arrange players so three overlapping two-person scenes exist along a line (positions 1-2, 2-3, 3-4...). Only the centre pair plays at a time. A director calls 'Pan left!' or 'Pan right!' and the active window slides to the next pair, who must instantly resume THEIR ongoing scene exactly where it paused. Cycle the camera back and forth so all scenes advance in fragments. Coach: hold each scene's reality in memory; pick up mid-beat with full energy.
variations: Split Screen (two scenes alternate on a clap); Zoom In/Zoom Out for nested scenes.

name: Standing Ovation
description: A guesser must discover three secret physical activities assigned by the group, guided only by audience cheers (hot) and boos (cold); trains physical experimentation and reading feedback.
instructions: One player leaves earshot; the group decides three specific physical actions for them to perform (hop on one foot, mime milking a cow, salute). The player returns knowing only that there are three actions, and starts physically trying things. The audience/group cheers louder as they get closer to a correct action and boos/'ehh's when off, building to a standing ovation when they nail each one. Coach the guesser: experiment boldly and commit; follow the energy.
origin: Drama-class / party-game tradition adopted by improv
variations: One activity for beginners; the actions form a connected sequence (a job).

name: Documentary
description: A long-form mockumentary structure: narration plus characters giving to-camera interviews about a place or event; trains narration, distinct characters, and confessional comedy.
instructions: Get a place or event suggestion. Open with a pattern of fake factoids and character declarations, ending on a title and tagline. Then alternate: a narrator gives documentary-style voiceover, scenes play out, and characters break to deliver direct-to-(invisible)-camera interview confessions introducing themselves and commenting on events. Build a connected story across the segments. Coach: interviews reveal what scenes hide; keep the narrator's tone wry and authoritative.
variations: Nature documentary about humans; true-crime docu-style; single-subject biography.

name: Splat
description: Fast circle reaction-elimination game where a pointed-at player ducks and their neighbors 'shoot' each other; trains reaction speed, focus, and playful elimination.
instructions: Circle with a leader in the middle. The leader points at a player saying 'Splat!'; that player must instantly duck while the two neighbors spin and 'shoot' each other ('Splat!') — the slower one is out. Misfires (ducking when not pointed at, shooting the wrong way) also eliminate you. Continue until two remain; finish with a back-to-back duel on a magic word. Keep the pace relentless. Coach: react, don't think.
variations: Cowboy theme; add sound-word variations; no-elimination practice version.

name: Bumpity Bump Bump Bump
description: Name-learning circle game: the center player demands a target's neighbors' names before finishing a fast phrase; trains name recall and calm under pressure.
instructions: Circle up; learn the names of the people on either side of you. The center player approaches anyone and says either '[Name], bumpity bump bump bump' (target must name their LEFT and RIGHT neighbors before the phrase ends) or just 'bumpity bump bump bump' (everyone must scramble to a new spot in the circle). Whoever fails or is caught without a spot goes to the center. Keep it fast. Coach: stay relaxed; panic kills recall.
variations: Categories instead of names (left = a fruit, right = a country); double-speed rounds.

name: Split Screen
description: Two separate scenes occupy opposite sides of the stage and play in alternation on a director's clap; trains thematic juxtaposition, scene memory, and instant pickup.
instructions: Set up two distinct scenes on left and right halves of the stage (e.g. a couple breaking up / a chef plating dessert). Only one side plays at a time; a director claps to 'switch channels', freezing one scene and reviving the other mid-beat. Alternate to let parallels and ironic juxtapositions emerge (one scene's line lands as a comment on the other). Coach: hold your frozen scene's reality so you can resume instantly; listen across the divide for resonances.
variations: Three-channel version; scenes that turn out to be connected (phone call across screens).

name: Rant
description: A player delivers an escalating first-person rant about a pet peeve; teammates tag in to continue and heighten the SAME emotion; trains commitment, heightening, and passionate speaking.
instructions: Get a topic (or use a real pet peeve). One player steps into the center and launches a fervent first-person rant ('People who don't return shopping carts...'). At any point a teammate tags them out and continues the same rant, raising the emotional pitch — not introducing a new complaint but escalating the existing one. Keep passing and heightening to a frenzy. Coach: heighten the feeling, don't change the subject; let your whole body rant.
origin: iO/UCB tag-monologue tradition; IRC Improv Wiki
variations: Solo timed version: rant on a random topic for 60 seconds without stopping; 'rave' positive-passion version; rant in gibberish then translate.

name: Cross the Circle (Yes)
description: Players cross the circle only after a teammate grants permission with eye contact and 'yes'; trains patient give-and-take, eye contact, and not moving until accepted.
instructions: Stand in a circle facing in. Player A makes eye contact with someone across the circle and points; that person says 'Yes' to acknowledge, and ONLY then may A walk to take their spot. Meanwhile the person who said 'Yes' must immediately find their own target, make eye contact, point, and wait for a 'Yes' before moving. Keep the chain flowing so players are constantly crossing without collisions. Coach: never move until you've received your 'yes' — it's a trust/timing drill.
variations: Name version (say the person's name to cross); add a second simultaneous crosser; gibberish greeting on each swap.

name: Yes-And / Yes-But / No
description: Partners plan the same event three times — once blocking with 'No', once hedging with 'Yes, but', once building with 'Yes, and' — to feel viscerally how agreement fuels collaboration.
instructions: Pairs plan an event (a holiday, a party). Round 1: respond to every suggestion with 'No, because...' and reject it. Round 2: respond with 'Yes, but...' (accept then undercut). Round 3: respond with 'Yes, and...' (accept and build). Use the SAME starting suggestion each round. Debrief how each felt — round 1 frustrating, round 2 stagnant, round 3 generative. Coach: notice the energy and where the plan actually goes somewhere.
variations: Group planning version; apply to a real disagreement to feel the shift.

name: Two-Headed Expert
description: Two players stand close and speak as a single expert in perfect unison, neither leading; an interviewer questions them; trains deep attunement and shared-mind speaking.
instructions: Two players become one two-headed person (referring to themselves as 'I', not 'we'). A third player interviews this expert on a topic. The two must speak EVERY word at exactly the same time, neither leading nor following — softening into a shared impulse, watching each other's mouths, keeping words short. Coach: don't try to control the sentence; relax and let the next word emerge between you; embrace the wrong-word collisions and justify them.
variations: Three-headed expert (one word each in sequence); two-headed-monster scene rather than interview.

name: Three-Headed Expert
description: Three players sit as one expert and answer interview questions one word at a time down the line; trains surrendering control of the sentence and accepting where it goes.
instructions: Three players sit shoulder to shoulder as a single expert being interviewed by a host. They answer each question by speaking ONE word each, left to right, repeating around as needed to form full sentences ('The' / 'secret' / 'is' / 'always' / 'butter'). No planning your word; serve the sentence. End sentences confidently rather than spiraling. Coach: short, clear words; commit to whatever sentence forms, even an absurd one.
variations: Three-headed Broadway star singing one word each; the host asks increasingly absurd questions.

name: Asides
description: Players break the fourth wall mid-scene to tell the audience their true thoughts, then return to the scene; trains subtext, comic contrast, and direct address.
instructions: Two players run a scene. At any moment a player may freeze the action (the partner holds), turn to the audience, and confess their character's real thoughts ('I cannot believe she's wearing that ring — it's MINE'), then snap back into the scene as if no time passed. Alternate asides. Coach: let the aside contradict what your character says aloud; keep asides short and pointed.
origin: Theatrical aside convention adopted by improv
variations: A director rings a bell to trigger asides; both players freeze and both confess simultaneously.

name: Mexican Name Wave
description: A stadium-style arm wave travels one way around the circle while names are passed the other way; trains split focus, coordination, and learning names.
instructions: Circle up. First establish a 'wave': one player raises both arms and lowers them; when their arms are fully up, the neighbor to the right starts theirs, sending a continuous wave around the circle. Once the wave flows, simultaneously pass names the OTHER direction: point to your left neighbor and say YOUR OWN name, and it travels left while the wave travels right. Coach: keep both patterns alive at once — that split attention is the workout.
variations: Send the name wave in the same direction as the arm wave; reverse both on a call.

name: Honey, I Love You
aliases: Honey If You Love Me Smile
description: Players try to make a straight-faced partner smile using only the line 'Honey, I love you, but I just can't smile'; trains commitment, playfulness, and composure under teasing.
instructions: Circle or pairs. The 'it' player approaches someone, makes eye contact, and says 'Honey, I love you, but I just can't smile' — using any voice, face, or gesture (short of touching) to crack them up. The target must reply 'Honey, I love you, but I just can't smile' WITHOUT smiling or laughing. If they smile, they become 'it'. Coach: commitment to the bit beats restraint; play with status, voice, and timing.
variations: Pairs staring contest version; the target must say a different straight line each time.

name: Energy Circle (Sound and Movement Pass)
description: A sound-plus-movement is created and copied around the circle, then a player can 'transform' it into a new one; the foundational copy-and-create physical warmup.
instructions: Circle up. Player 1 makes a distinct sound paired with a movement and 'sends' it to their neighbor, who copies it exactly and passes the copy on around the circle. When the original returns to Player 1 (or whenever a player chooses), that player TRANSFORMS it into a brand-new sound-and-movement and sends that around. Continue, alternating faithful copying and bold transformation. Coach: copy fully (don't water it down), then commit hard to your new creation.
variations: Pass the Face (facial expressions only); send two different sound-motions in opposite directions; emotion-and-movement version.

name: Convergence (Group Mind Meld)
description: The whole group counts down together and each shouts a word, repeating until the entire ensemble converges on one shared word; a harder group-wide version of Mind Meld.
instructions: Whole group stands in a circle. Count '1, 2, 3' together; on '3' everyone simultaneously shouts any single word. Then, thinking of a word that links what you heard, count down again and everyone shouts a new word — aiming for the group to collapse toward one common word. No talking between rounds, no repeating used words. Continue until the entire group says the SAME word at once (cue celebration). Coach: average toward the most obvious link, don't be clever.
variations: Pairs Mind Meld feeding into a whole-group hive mind; converge on a gesture instead of a word.

name: Cut To
description: Players (or a director) call 'Cut to...' to jump the story to a new time, place, or flashback like film editing; trains narrative editing and instant scene establishment.
instructions: Run a scene. Any player or a director can call 'Cut to...' and name a new moment ('Cut to: three years later', 'Cut to: the same night across town', 'Cut to: a flashback of their first meeting'). The cast instantly transforms the stage into that new scene and plays it, then can cut again. Use cuts to skip boring connective tissue and juxtapose times/places. Coach: cut TO something meaningful (a consequence, a contrast), not randomly; establish the new scene in the first line.
variations: Match-cut version (the new scene starts on the same image/word); flashback-only round; smash-cut for comedy.

name: Object Naming Speed Round
description: Players point at real or imaginary objects and rapidly call them by the WRONG name; trains breaking habitual associations and quieting the literal mind.
instructions: Walk around (or stand in a circle) pointing at objects and naming each one with a word that is NOT what it is ('door' -> 'banana', 'chair' -> 'ocean'). Go as fast as you can without repeating names or saying the correct one; a stumble or a real name resets a counter. Speed forces your brain off autopilot. Coach: don't search for clever wrong names — say the first non-matching word that comes.
origin: Cognitive-flexibility drill used in improv and acting classes
variations: Name each object as the previous object you named; partner points and you name; category constraint (all wrong names must be animals).

name: Last Word, First Word
description: Each line of dialogue must begin with the LAST word of the partner's previous line; trains end-of-sentence listening and fluid pickups.
instructions: Pairs scene from a suggestion. Whatever word your partner's line ENDS on must be the first word of your next line ('...I just need some peace' -> 'Peace is exactly what they want you to think'). Keep the scene's story and relationship alive despite the constraint. Buzz/swap on errors in performance, or self-correct in practice. Coach: you literally cannot pre-plan, so listen all the way to the final word.
variations: Last letter version (covered separately); three-player chain; the repeated word must change meaning.

name: Restaurant Quirks
description: A diner (or pair of diners) must guess the secret quirks of a parade of servers; a restaurant-themed Party Quirks variant that trains indirect characterization.
instructions: One or two players sit as restaurant patrons. A series of servers enters one at a time, each with a secret quirk/identity (a waiter who narrates everything as a sportscast; one who is slowly turning into a cat). Servers play the quirk fully while taking the order, never naming it; the diners try to guess each quirk, sending correct ones 'off shift'. Coach servers: escalate clues subtle-to-broad; coach diners: play the meal, not an interrogation.
variations: Job-interview quirks; doctor's-office quirks; the diners also have quirks.

name: Sit-Stand-Kneel-Lie
description: Four players run a scene where one must always be sitting, one standing, one kneeling, and one lying down; a four-person extension of Sit/Stand/Lie that trains stage picture and rebalancing.
instructions: Four players, any suggestion. At every moment the four must occupy four distinct levels: sitting, standing, kneeling, and lying down. Whenever one player changes position, the others must instantly rebalance so all four levels are covered, justifying their moves inside the story. Keep the scene's relationships primary; the physical puzzle is secondary. Coach: justify the WHY of every move; don't just mechanically swap.
variations: Three-level version (the original); add a fifth position; levels assigned by the audience.

name: Park Bench
description: Players take turns approaching a person on a park bench, each entering with a strong pre-chosen character and an endowment for the seated player; trains scene initiation and instant relationship.
instructions: Set one chair as a park bench. One player sits, neutral. A second player enters having already decided who THEY are and who the person on the bench is, and starts a short interaction that establishes both characters and a relationship. The first player reacts and discovers who they've been made into, then finds a reason to leave. Now the second player stays and a third approaches with a new character and a new endowment. Continue cycling. Coach: enter with a clear who/what/why and give your bench partner a strong identity in your first lines.
variations: Bus stop or waiting-room setting; the seated player must justify whatever endowment they receive; two benches running in parallel.

name: Endowment Circle
description: A player must deduce a secret trait, identity, or occupation that everyone else knows, from how the others treat them; trains reading subtext and indirect communication.
instructions: One player steps out while the group secretly decides an endowment for them — a job, relationship, mood, physical trait, or who they are ('a famous magician', 'someone everyone secretly pities'). The player returns into a scene; the others treat them entirely consistent with the endowment WITHOUT stating it. The player picks up on the treatment, plays along, and tries to figure out (and eventually voice) who/what they are. The group/audience 'oohs' as they get warmer. Coach: communicate through behavior and how you address them, never by announcing.
variations: Gibberish endowment guess (physical trait, job, emotion); endowment written on a card on the player's back at a mingle party.

name: Genre Rollercoaster
description: One continuous scene whose genre is changed repeatedly by a caller; players must instantly shift style while keeping the same story moving; trains genre fluency and adaptability.
instructions: Gather a list of genres from the audience and an opening offer. Players begin a scene in a neutral style for a few beats to set the premise. A caller then announces a genre ('Horror!', 'Bollywood musical!', 'Film noir!') and the players immediately transform the SAME ongoing story into that style — language, physicality, pacing, music — then carry on until the next genre is called. Continue through several calls to a finish. Coach: don't restart the story at each call; recolor the story you already have.
variations: Players call the genre changes themselves; spin a wheel of genres; emotion rollercoaster instead of genres.

name: Slow-Motion Commentary
description: Two players perform an everyday action in dramatic slow motion while two others give live sports-style commentary; trains heightening the mundane and confident play-by-play speaking.
instructions: Two players slowly mime an ordinary event in extreme slow motion (making a sandwich, a breakup, a job interview). Two commentators narrate it as if it's a high-stakes sporting event, with play-by-play and color commentary, building tension and stakes around tiny gestures ('And he reaches for the mayonnaise — bold choice, Jim!'). Swap roles. Coach commentators: treat trivial moves as epic; commit to broadcaster energy and jargon.
variations: One commentator plus expert analyst; nature-documentary commentary instead of sports; instant-replay of the best moment.

name: Restaurant Two Tables
description: Two simultaneous restaurant-table scenes share a waiter who moves between them, carrying lines and energy across; trains juggling parallel scenes and connecting them through one character.
instructions: Set two tables with two diners each on opposite sides of the stage. A single waiter (the connective character) moves between tables. Only the table the waiter is at plays actively; the other freezes. As the waiter crosses, the active scene switches. Let what the waiter overhears at one table inform what they bring to the other, weaving the two conversations together. Coach: the waiter is the thread — carry tone and information between tables to create irony and connection.
variations: Three tables; the diners' stories turn out to be linked; the waiter's mood infects both tables.

name: Gibberish Endowment Guess
description: A player returns to a gibberish scene and must guess three secret endowments (a physical trait, a job, an emotion) from teammates' gibberish and behavior; trains nonverbal reading and inference.
instructions: One player leaves; the group gets three endowments for them from the audience — a physical characteristic, an occupation, and an emotion. The player returns into a scene where EVERYONE (including them) speaks only gibberish. Teammates convey the three endowments purely through gibberish tone, gesture, and how they treat the player, who acts on what they sense and eventually mimes/guesses each endowment. The audience 'oohs' as they get close. Coach: communicate via physicality and emotional tone, since words are off the table.
variations: English version (Party Quirks); guess only one endowment for beginners.
